quoted_text:
高端的加密盗窃，只需要最简单的手段。

今年大家都在担心 AI 的迅猛发展会破解钱包私钥，但是目前最有效的盗窃其实没这么高端，比如直接在卖硬件钱包的下游经销商那做手脚，也就是供应链攻击。

最近发生的近 9100 万美元的 Ledger 钱包被盗案就是这个手法。

马来西亚有一家叫 CryptoBilis 的硬件钱包商店，自 2022 年起就是 Ledger 官方授权的东南亚经销商。

这家店卖的确实是正品，积累了多年的真实客户。然而今年春天，创始人把店悄悄卖给了一位新老板，商店表面上一切如常，继续顶着“Ledger 官方授权”的牌子卖货。

但前几天，研究者@MagicalTux拆了一台从这家店买来的 Ledger 发现，设备内部被魔改了。

偷窃者根本没有去破解 Ledger 的安全芯片（，而是在屏幕下方偷偷塞进了一块带有 LTE 调制解调器和 eSIM 卡的微型电路板。

这块微型板子只做一件事：盯着屏幕。当你满心欢喜地设置新钱包，屏幕上依次显示 24 个助记词时，它就直接通过移动网络把这些词发送回黑客手里。

就是这么朴实无华且有效...

Ledger 的硬件钱包没问题，卖货渠道没问题，一切防不胜防。

如果你的钱包来自第三方渠道，强烈建议去官网找拆解教程，打开外壳看看有没有多余的电路板。

最稳妥的办法是直接从官网买个新设备，生成全新的助记词并转移资产。

永远不要考验人性，官网直购才是王道。

$EMBER is more than just a Solana launchpad. It is expanding across multiple chains while gradually building its brand, community, and token economy.

5dvXTZ5qwgafnHtwu3Ls3QrWx1U4LQsFeCuJgkk4QEC6

EMBER has now expanded into five on-chain product environments, spanning Solana, Robinhood Chain, Halcyon, and Orca Whirlpools, aiming to grow its business through different launch mechanisms and liquidity products across ecosystems.

On the tokenomics side, EMBER initially prioritized reward distribution, returning value to the community before introducing a burn mechanism following a community vote. The team emphasizes that revenue, community distributions, buybacks, and burns are publicly trackable, and plans to move into its next phase in Q4.

The real opportunity for EMBER lies in whether it can sustainably grow trading volume and fee revenue, while generating actual token demand through mechanisms such as buybacks and burns. Cross-chain expansion and community governance strengthen the long-term narrative, but trading volume is not the same as revenue, and token burns do not automatically translate into price appreciation. text:
这次交流，有两个比较深的印象🤔

一个关于概念与落地。

听老师们聊起 AI、TradFi、支付，都说明显感觉到了推背感。

说概念的时候，都非常天马行空。但话题回到实际体验的时候，确实很自然地聊到了币安的产品。

这个转场就让人感受到，讲故事可能确实更快，但最终能留住用户的，还是真正解决实际问题的产品。怎么把市场对未来的想象，变成用户触手可及的现实，这中间看似只有一步，却往往是最难的。

另外一个印象，关于倾听。

越来越觉得，认真倾听是交流的第一原则😂只有认真听，才能从一些蛛丝马迹里找到线索，顺着线索，才能打开话匣子。线索越深，听到的东西也越具体。

比如，有人说自己一直没弄懂某些交易活动该怎么参加。又比如，有人感受到今年产品更新明显更快了，但有些新功能其实还没来得及体验.......

这些都是很具体，不说就容易被忽略的问题。但知道了，我们就可以思考是不是可以多做一些简单直接的教程，是不是继续优化邀请和体验机制等等

交流下来就会觉得，你听得越认真，对方越愿意掏心掏肺，对方说得越真实，我们也越容易发现那些可以继续做得更好的细节。确实有收获，再次感谢各位老师🙏

text:
ARR 是今天 AI 创业最危险的增长幻觉。

最近 USV 合伙人 Mike Mignano 在 Sourcery 的访谈里，重新谈起了自己此前那个很有争议的观点：

ARR is a fake metric。

我去看了完整的 85 分钟对谈，发现他们真正担心的问题，比 ARR 本身有意思得多。

Mignano 说，现在让用户为 AI 产品掏钱实在太容易了。各种订阅制、年费套餐，有些产品甚至不付钱就没法完整体验。

一个用户可能因为看了一段 Demo，或者在 Twitter 上刷到几条推荐，就直接购买了一年的会员。

公司拿到了收入，ARR 开始增长，融资故事也有了。但这个用户可能第二周就再也没打开过产品。

Rebecca Kaden 在节目里也提到了一个现象，AI 消费市场正在经历极高的尝鲜率和极低的实际参与度。

我觉得这恰好击中了这一轮 AI 应用创业最微妙的问题。

过去我们会把付费看作需求得到验证的重要信号。但今天，AI 产品的传播速度、开发速度和商业化速度都在大幅提高，用户形成稳定习惯的速度却没有同步加快。

一家创业公司可能只需要几个月，就能做出漂亮的收入曲线。但要证明用户一年后仍然愿意使用它，真的需要一年。

于是产生了一个非常荒诞的局面：

资本可以提前给公司未来几年的增长定价，用户却可能连下个月还用不用这个产品都没想好。

而且 AI 应用还有另一个麻烦。

USV 在访谈里反复讨论网络效应。当年他们投资 Twitter，看中的是每增加一个用户，整个网络就会变得更有价值。

但今天大量 AI Agent 仍然是单人使用的工具，模型能力又在不断趋同。用户可能很喜欢某款产品，但只要明天有个更便宜、更好用的替代品，迁移成本就很低。

这意味着，一部分 AI 公司即使证明了用户愿意付钱，也还没证明自己有能力长期留住这些用户。

最有意思的是，USV 恰好刚刚募集了历史上规模最大的 9 亿美元基金。

投资人一边怀疑增长数据，一边又不得不更早、更大规模地下注。

因为等到留存、复购、网络效应都被充分验证，真正的赢家可能早已贵得买不起了。

我甚至觉得，AI 正在让一级市场出现一种新的错配，产品越来越容易被验证为「有人愿意付钱」，却越来越难被验证为「有人愿意一直用」。

所以我现在看 AI 应用的收入纪录，越来越不关心它用了几个月做到 1000 万美元 ARR。

我更想知道，有多少用户在第 90 天还会主动打开它？有多少用户会在年费到期后续订？如果明天 ChatGPT 免费提供同样的功能，还有多少人愿意留下？

这些问题没那么适合做融资新闻，但可能比那些漂亮的 ARR 数字更接近一家公司的真实价值。

text:
Jeff Yan: TradFi's Speed Arms Race Is Zero-Sum — and Even Negative-Sum

Hyperliquid Labs co-founder Jeff Yan @chameleon_jeff  said at DAS Asia 2026 on October 7 that he does not view Hyperliquid’s priority fee mechanism as “bribery.” Its purpose, he said, is to reduce advantages from low-latency infrastructure and make genuine trading alpha more important. 

Yan argued that the latency race in traditional finance — involving microwave towers and transatlantic fiber cables — is fundamentally zero-sum, and sometimes even negative-sum, because it creates little meaningful value. Hyperliquid aims to use priority fees to internalize these negative externalities, allowing traders to compete more fairly without spending heavily on low-latency infrastructure.

高端的加密盗窃，只需要最简单的手段。

今年大家都在担心 AI 的迅猛发展会破解钱包私钥，但是目前最有效的盗窃其实没这么高端，比如直接在卖硬件钱包的下游经销商那做手脚，也就是供应链攻击。

最近发生的近 9100 万美元的 Ledger 钱包被盗案就是这个手法。

马来西亚有一家叫 CryptoBilis 的硬件钱包商店，自 2022 年起就是 Ledger 官方授权的东南亚经销商。

这家店卖的确实是正品，积累了多年的真实客户。然而今年春天，创始人把店悄悄卖给了一位新老板，商店表面上一切如常，继续顶着“Ledger 官方授权”的牌子卖货。

但前几天，研究者@MagicalTux拆了一台从这家店买来的 Ledger 发现，设备内部被魔改了。

偷窃者根本没有去破解 Ledger 的安全芯片（，而是在屏幕下方偷偷塞进了一块带有 LTE 调制解调器和 eSIM 卡的微型电路板。

这块微型板子只做一件事：盯着屏幕。当你满心欢喜地设置新钱包，屏幕上依次显示 24 个助记词时，它就直接通过移动网络把这些词发送回黑客手里。

就是这么朴实无华且有效...

Ledger 的硬件钱包没问题，卖货渠道没问题，一切防不胜防。

如果你的钱包来自第三方渠道，强烈建议去官网找拆解教程，打开外壳看看有没有多余的电路板。

最稳妥的办法是直接从官网买个新设备，生成全新的助记词并转移资产。

永远不要考验人性，官网直购才是王道。

3，用 Gmail 邮箱登陆注册 ，我一直没弹身份验证，不知道是不是机率问题。

4，如果在网页上注册google 的 Gmail账号会要验证等 ，很麻烦，所以我用 ipad 端或手机端的 Gmail app 注册帐号就会跳过很多验证。

5，本机 新Claude号在用的时候，很多人说要注意本机的语言时区啥的 N 多问题，但我现在有个号，是破罐子破摔法。。。啥也没设置，只是把以前的 Claude code 和 Claude 桌面端全删干净了（用的 Mole软件）然后就这样用，啥时候封了，啥时候算，现在已经两个月了，屁事没有。

所以说，有时候真的邪门！ 

6，我只在美区苹果商城订阅（安卓听说也可以），因为被封号了很快能要回来钱，写申请也没那么复杂，就说号被限制使用了，申请退款。100%退回来，还没有一次没给我钱。

7，用过很多方法想让更多团队的人使用 Claude , 所以试着让 claude 和飞书打通，这样，飞书上的同事就可以与它对话，但走的是一个帐号的输入入口。我感觉这个事情还行（只用与对话）

但注册的时候，我用的是浏览器无痕模式。

最后，我不知道上面的是经验，还是教训，或者过不久就没啥用了，你们比照一下，看看是不是有点用处。

当然，你自己判断，别被封号了，回来骂我。。。因为我已经身心疲惫，满身伤痕。。。。。

author: wilderko
quoted_text:
Disappointed by the European Central Bank’s (ECB) and European Banking Authority’s (EBA) responses to the MiCA consultation.

They are not only advocating for a prohibition on paying yield on stablecoins, but also for restrictions on CASPs providing access to DeFi, including protocols offering yield on non-MiCA-authorized stablecoins, without providing a clear framework for how access to DeFi should work in practice.

They also suggest that CASPs offering access to DeFi should restrict it to certain groups of users through so-called “suitability tests,” alongside a potential certification regime for DeFi lending protocols.

It is unclear how these requirements would work in practice. If regulators determine which protocols are deemed suitable for European users, the result risks looking very different from the open DeFi that exists today.

Instead, we could end up with more walled gardens that undermine the liquidity and network effects of open financial networks, ultimately limiting Europeans’ ability to access new ways to grow and preserve wealth.

These proposals are presented as measures to “protect consumers.” But excessive restrictions can instead create more friction for innovation and slow the development of open, transparent, and auditable financial infrastructure that can benefit consumers.

The reality is that onchain finance, including stablecoins, DeFi, and tokenized securities, has the potential to reshape financial infrastructure by reducing friction, increasing transparency, and expanding access to financial opportunities.

European consumers and businesses stand to benefit significantly from this transformation, particularly if the companies building this infrastructure can continue to build and compete from within Europe.

Meanwhile, U.S. regulators, including the SEC and CFTC, have increasingly taken a more pragmatic approach toward enabling onchain financial innovation.

European regulators should put users and their interests at the center of the framework. Banks and other incumbents should be able to adapt their businesses to serve users in an increasingly onchain economy, rather than relying on artificial restrictions that risk increasing costs and reducing access for Europeans as the rest of the world moves onchain.

DeFi will win.

text:
If you hold 1,000 near:native  and don’t stake it, you’ll still have 1,000 next year. 

You’ll just own about 2.4% less of the network. About 90K new NEAR gets created every day and most of it goes to stakers.

@sal_ternullo’s proposal says 58.7% of NEAR isn’t staked. So most of the supply is in that first row.

If you stake, you end the year with about 1,047, and your share goes up by a bit less than the non-staker’s went down, because your validator takes a cut. That’s where the yield comes from.

and the @Bitwise’s NRR ETF - has a net staking rate of 3.3% and a 0.75% fee. That leaves about 2.5% a year, which is almost exactly what the network prints.

So the ETF holder ends up about flat. The staking covers the dilution and the fee, and not much else.

The cut that’s trending today would take that 2.4% down to about 1.6% over two years, and the staking yield down by about a third.

If you want the middle row, staking is a few clicks in most NEAR wallets: pick a validator and delegate. Getting back out takes two to three days.

Staking doesn’t get you a vote on the cut, though. The proposal is still a draft and voting hasn’t opened. To vote you have to lock NEAR in House of Stake before it clears screening.

None of this is about price, btw, it’s what happens to your slice.

https://t.co/bbo7rYCPtm

author: EulerLagrange

text:
Treasury 2023 De-risking Strategy: BSA compliance costs (due diligence, monitoring) make low-volume foreign retail accounts unprofitable, so institutions drop entire jurisdictions/customers. Same BSA framework (AML programs, CIP, SARs) applies to securities brokers.

Fink 2025 letter: “tokenized funds will become as familiar… provided we crack one critical problem: identity verification… championing tokenization alone won’t suffice. We must solve digital verification, too.”

Tokenization does not solve the barriers. Buying available exposure shows demand for the asset despite ownership limits, not low demand for ownership.

Brother Eli generating value, then putting some of it back in the hands of the people actually supporting it.

text:
K 线有三种关系：绝对关系、相对关系和逻辑关系。

第一种绝对关系，就是 K 线之间OHLC 之间的绝对差异值，也是大多数交易者学习技术分析时的基点

第二种相对关系是有机的组合k 线区间，把它当成一部分行情来看，同时也会看待目标 k 线和其他标的之间的强弱关系

量化交易能处理的K 线到前两种就为止了。想要处理第三种逻辑关系，难度等于搓一个小型的大模型出来

第三种逻辑关系是部分 K 线表现在整个价格发展中的逻辑。猪猪老师说过一句话，叫“想清楚每根 K 线背后发生了什么”，其实也是一种找到 K 线之间逻辑关系。这种研究本质是捕捉 K 线后的资金流，通过资金流推断出每个参与者成分的意图，通过盘面留下的蛛丝马迹，推断出整体的资金导向

这三种关系的递进，逐渐从个体转向整体，倒逼到行情发展的本质。这个过程是困难的，因为想看懂下一层关系，需要学习很多 k 线之外的知识。就逻辑关系而言，我个人现在也只能看懂极少数标的的极少数行情发展

有意思的是，我认为有一种简单朴素的方法贯穿了这三条，它就是趋势线。趋势线里包含了K 线的绝对关系、相对关系和逻辑关系。比如一段更高的高点，更高的低点，一段强势的承接，一段该涨不涨的抛压。趋势线就像平面几何里的辅助线一样，帮我们简化了问题，虽然靠一条辅助线本身还不足以解答出题目，但是可以把这个复杂的高维问题投射到我们熟悉的坐标轴上

更有意思的是，我和 Eric 讨论过不止一次趋势线的策略设想，我们最终发现，量化策略没有办法把这条线画出来。无论是用均价的替代，还是规定高低点划线，都无法像人脑那样画出一条这么模糊又这么清晰的趋势线。

或许这就是人脑处理上的优势吧

Let's talk about $JEANPHIL and $CLAUDIA, and why I'm bullish on the AI Influencer + short-form video narrative.

GTBxUiw6wJdmmkCGZgRHLyYxqu1vG4KtRpeox6yDpump 
2j5SaS7xy776qCBpyPQbZjyQSAtKiFgrwjfErthnW2ZM 

First, the broader sector.

I believe AI Influencers combined with short-form video distribution could become one of the narratives worth watching in the next Meme market cycle.

The underlying logic is simple: AI is turning character creation from a high-cost, low-frequency process into a low-cost, scalable content business that can be operated continuously. In the past, building an influencer required appearance, performance, filming, editing, and long-term management. Now, creators can use AI to design characters, develop personalities, produce short videos, and even operate multiple virtual personas simultaneously.

But what really matters isn't how many characters AI can generate. It's whether those characters can consistently produce content that people want to watch, discuss, and follow.

Short-form video drives distribution, characters accumulate attention, and Memes can become a speculative vehicle for that attention in the crypto market. An AI character can build a distinctive persona through continuous video releases, participate in trending topics, create new memes, and interact with other characters, gradually evolving from a single viral clip into a recognizable IP.

Compared with traditional Memes that rely on an isolated event or a single image, these characters theoretically have the ability to continuously generate new material for distribution. If a character develops a stable audience and cultural recognition, it no longer has to rely entirely on a single viral moment to maintain attention.

If this model gains traction in the crypto market, speculation may shift beyond the next viral image toward AI characters that have already attracted genuine attention on platforms like TikTok and Instagram, can consistently produce content, and have the potential to channel that external attention on-chain.

This is why I've chosen to take a deeper look at JEANPHIL and CLAUDIA. They represent two different paths within this emerging narrative.

JEANPHIL: External traction that has already emerged.

Jean Phil is an AI-generated French male character. His blond bowl cut, curled mustache, brown houndstooth suit, and signature street-style boxing moves create a recognizable visual identity that is easy to imitate.

The character has attracted significant attention on TikTok and Instagram, generating imitations and derivative content. This demonstrates how an AI character with a distinctive persona and a simple, replicable video format can quickly capture attention on mainstream social platforms.

The logic is straightforward: the character attracts external traffic, the content inspires imitations and remixes, and that attention may eventually flow into its on-chain token.

Compared with Memes that rely solely on narratives originating within crypto, JEANPHIL already has an external source of attention. What it needs to prove next is whether that momentum can persist and whether the character's popularity can translate into sustained token demand.

CLAUDIA: From AI creation toward long-term IP development.

CLAUDIA is more focused on long-term IP development. Around Claudia, anabology has been building Claudia Gallery and proposed creating an open version of Hatsune Miku for the AI era. Related initiatives also include AI character creation tools, Agent Skills, and Claudia Local.

The Influencer mode brings this vision closer to the AI Influencer model: by continuously producing videos, maintaining a consistent character identity, and experimenting with high-frequency publishing, it aims to gradually build its own audience.

The logic is that AI lowers content production costs, continuous video output helps establish character recognition, and the character gradually accumulates an audience before attempting to convert that external attention into IP influence and on-chain interest.

Compared with JEANPHIL, CLAUDIA has greater potential in the direction of a long-term AI creator ecosystem. The goal isn't simply to make a character go viral in the short term, but to explore how an AI character can continuously produce content, build an audience, and develop into an expandable, open IP.

However, this path has a longer chain of validation. Being able to produce videos consistently doesn't mean the content will necessarily gain traction. Having creation tools doesn't guarantee the ability to build a successful character. And an open-IP vision doesn't automatically mean the token can capture the resulting value.

Although both projects fall under the broader AI Influencer narrative, their trading theses are different.

JEANPHIL is more focused on existing external traction. The key question is whether that attention can persist and translate into token demand. CLAUDIA is more focused on AI creation capabilities and long-term IP development. The key question is whether it can consistently produce compelling content and build a genuine audience.

What I'm bullish on is the shared potential behind both approaches: AI characters could evolve beyond static images into dynamic IPs that continuously produce content, participate in trending topics, build social relationships, and generate new Memes.

Of course, a compelling sector narrative doesn't mean every related token will appreciate.

We need to distinguish three separate outcomes: an AI character gaining attention, an IP building lasting influence, and a token capturing value from that influence. A character can become popular without benefiting its token. A project can have impressive creation tools without producing viral content. Even if an IP continues to grow, attention may remain entirely off-chain if the token has no meaningful connection to its development.

Therefore, what I'm really looking for isn't the first token to announce that it uses AI, but projects that have demonstrated their ability to attract external attention, consistently produce distributable content, and establish a clear connection between that attention and their tokens.

AI is the production tool, short-form video is the distribution channel, character IP is the vehicle for attention, and the token represents a separate speculative market.

When these four elements become genuinely connected, AI Influencers could evolve from a trending concept into a new Meme narrative with sustained distribution potential.

In my view, the projects most likely to break out will need a distinctive character identity, consistent content distribution, a genuine external audience, and a mechanism for translating attention into token demand. That's why I'm bullish on this direction and have chosen to take a deeper look at JEANPHIL and CLAUDIA.

JEANPHIL Chart:https://t.co/Ub5wHq0ObA

text:
Assorted things I've been mulling over regarding agents in the economy:

• Companies are in some sense the original superintelligence. It's often the case that they can use their amortized cognitive surplus to advance their interests against those of certain consumers: relative to the optimization capacity of companies, consumers can be inattentive, underinformed, irrational, etc. (Think, say, of some of the classic insurance upsells at the end of a booking process, which is typically priced substantially above what a regular policy would cost.) Herbert Simon introduced the idea of bounded rationality, and firms often end up benefiting from it. Thanks to personal agents, we will probably get somewhat more rational in how we engage with companies.

• How exactly will outcomes change? Well, certain kinds of price discrimination will work less well (how do coupons work if every agent hunts fastidiously for them?), and certain kinds of customer cross-subsidy will change (today, people who forget to cancel subscriptions subsidize those who don't). Taken across the economy as a whole, I'm not sure what the incidence of all of this will be.

• In corporate strategy, people have long debated the relative importance of distribution and product quality. Perhaps you've made something better, but does anyone know about it? Won't people just continue to buy the ACME Corp Mousetraps? Personal agents will, I think, act as a kind of structural subsidy for product quality. How would markets look different if individuals always spent at least 10 hours researching their purchases? On the margin, focusing on making a product better is, I think, going to become a more effective strategy for companies. This is good!

• It true, a corollary is that information about product quality will become more important and impactful. Today, most people have very limited ability to aggregate and integrate such data, but agents will have insatiable thirst for such signals. (It's often said that data is becoming more valuable because it helps in the training of models. That's obviously true, but I think there's a secondary way in which it's more valuable simply as a complement to cheaper intelligence.)

• A big question is whether agents will increase superstar effects (rational agents all settle on the same product) or increase dispersion (because everyone has slightly different tastes and preferences, which agents are good at eliciting, finally overcoming the artificial clustering we've been subjected to).

• Many internet companies have monetized demand routing, which is in turn often predicated on short attention spans. "I'll click on the first thing I see." This has led to some amount of inefficiency, as companies try to propitiate capricious ranking algorithms and incur various placement fees. It's not all deadweight loss (willingness to pay is itself a kind of signal, which is valuable to buyers), but it's not great. How will the nature and value of this routing change in a world of personal agents? I don't know the answer, but I think that the effects might be pretty big.

• Much of what I'm writing hinges on the assumption that personal agents will be on the consumer's side. I suspect that that will be the winning strategy, but whether it's true, and what it means to be true, involves a lot of other questions.

Taken as a whole, the market is a massively parallelized, decentralized, and highly imperfect value attribution machine, and, taking stock of all of the effects, it seems to me that the quality point may well be the biggest: that agents will change the nature of the backpropagation such that the rewards for better products increase. Maybe this is too optimistic, but I suspect (and hope) that companies that make things that they're proud of will feel that the universe is a little more partisan in their favor.

据XRP Ledger官方披露，xrpld 3.4.1版本修复了一个支付引擎整数溢出漏洞。攻击者可通过数百个特制挂单加一笔支付凭空增发XRP并正常花费，还能绕过"不增发XRP"的安全检查，增发量可远超XRP总供应量。该漏洞或自2015年起就已存在。

研究人员于9月22日通过漏洞赏金计划提交该漏洞，3.4.1版本于9月25日发布，目前未发现被利用迹象。

只喊不买是大忽悠，只买不喊是闷声发财，而又买又喊，才是明牌阳谋。

最近TOKEN2049 期间，Tom Lee 在接受访谈时，又喊出 $ETH 本轮牛市有望达到 2.5 万至 5 万美元，年底先看5000 美元。

看多了他喊单也就会心一笑，但如果只把这个当口嗨那就想简单了。

实际上 Tom Lee 是真的又喊又买，并且大部分的 ETH 建仓都在熊市完成了。

作为美股上市公司 BitMine 的董事会主席，Tom Lee 早在 2025 年 6 月底就正式启动了一项极其激进的以太坊财库计划，代号为“Alchemy of 5%”（5% 炼金术）。

当时他们立下的目标是要拿下以太坊全网流通供应量的 5%，结果他们只用了 15 个月就几乎达成了目标。

截至目前，BitMine 手里已经囤积了约 601.6 万枚 ETH，占以太坊流通总量的 4.9%，距离 5% 的硬性上限只差最后不到 10 万枚。

复盘他的成本线，BitMine 的综合持仓成本大致在 3300 至 3600 美元 之间。

这意味着在今年以太坊深度回调、一度跌破 1800 美元甚至更低的至暗时刻，他们的账面浮亏曾高达几十亿甚至近百亿美元。

换作普通散户早已割肉离场，一般的机构也早该停止建仓装死。

但他们和微策略基本一致，利用美股股权增发募集现金，在熊市下跌中逆势加仓，同时把买来的大部分 ETH 质押赚取稳健现金流，把浮亏阶段变成了收集廉价筹码的黄金窗口。

所以，对 Bitmine 而言建仓已经接近尾声，筹码已经吃饱，接下来最重要的任务，就是把叙事天花板喊到极致，唤醒二级市场的做多情绪。

text:
New paper from Kalshi about its traders demolishes myths about prediction markets:

> Traders who bet on sports tend to be from ZIP codes with *higher* incomes vs. those who bet on non-sports

> The median income of traders is right around the national average

> 82% of top traders do not have finance backgrounds

> 65% of top traders say that they are mostly or entirely self-taught

> 91% of top traders are not full-time traders, and most hold full-time jobs elsewhere

Yet top traders are highly skilled:

> About 31% of top traders get a perfect score on a probability test, compared to just 2% of the population

> Top traders showed wide-ranging variation in confidence on different bets, compared to the general population, whose confidence levels were relatively flat

> 62% of top traders actively look for sources that contradict their view

> 64% say that they try to figure out what they missed when their prediction failed

> Top traders are much better educated than the general population

This paper helps to explain why prediction markets are highly predictive of actual outcomes and serve a valuable purpose for society; they aggregate information much more efficiently than standard polling methods, and are more often correct.

What type of people are successful on Kalshi?

We commissioned an independent third party to study our top traders. Here’s what they found:

Top traders are not limited to privileged or financial backgrounds.
-79% went to public school
-They are over 2x as likely to have worked retail or service jobs than on Wall Street
-65% are self-taught

The majority of top traders: :
-Actively seek out primary documents for research
-Actively seek out conflicting sources to challenge their beliefs
-Outperform the public on numeracy tests

The findings echo the foundational work of Philip Tetlock: the best forecasters are not subject matter experts. They tend to be otherwise-ordinary people who are intellectually humble, willing to do research, and think probabilistically instead of emotionally.

text:
Official XRPL vulnerability disclosure report published October 9, 2026. 

What happened

A researcher (Cayden Liao and Veria AI) reported an integer-overflow bug in the payment engine through the XRPL Bug Bounty program on September 22, 2026. It affected xrpld 3.4.0 and earlier and dated back to when the current payment engine was written in 2015. 

How it worked: When a payment consumed many offers from the order book, the engine summed the amounts the buyer owed using plain 64-bit integer addition with no overflow check. A few hundred specially crafted offers (each selling a tiny amount of a token for a very large amount of XRP) could make the total wrap around to a small number. The engine still paid each offer owner the full amount but charged the buyer only the wrapped-around total effectively minting the difference as new, spendable XRP.

Two existing safeguards failed for the same reason:
•  The built-in “no XRP created” invariant check used the same unchecked 64-bit summing and also wrapped around, so it saw only the normal transaction fee.
•  Per-account balance limits only trigger if one account exceeds the total supply; spreading the minted XRP across many attacker-controlled accounts kept each under the limit.

The attack required unnatural offer prices that no real trader would use and a payment deliberately built to consume them all at once. It could not be triggered by ordinary trading or payments. Cost was low (account/offer reserves plus fees).

Fix and impact

The fix shipped in the emergency xrpld 3.4.1 release on September 25, 2026. The payment engine now checks for overflow when summing offer amounts; if it would overflow, that part of the payment fails cleanly (path dry / partial payment). The invariant checker was also upgraded to a wider counter, and related summing paths were hardened. 
Because of the severity (cheap, no special access, and able to mint spendable XRP), this change was applied immediately on upgrade rather than going through the normal multi-week amendment process. Validators upgraded rapidly (>80% of the default UNL on release day). The source code was withheld briefly and has since been published.

No evidence of exploitation on any public network.

The same 3.4.1 release also fixed a separate Batch-transaction wrapper validation issue (fixBatchV1_2 amendment, which activated on mainnet today). Older servers are now amendment-blocked and must upgrade to stay in sync.

IMO: Nobody knows what effect this has had on the supply.

text:
Seventy years ago today, America welcomed my dad (pictured center) and his family as Palestinian Christian refugees. It was the greatest blessing of his life.

Born Attallah Amash in 1940, my dad had an extremely difficult childhood. He was a victim of war, expelled from his home at just eight years old in 1948, moving from place to place to find shelter and living off scraps.

He never had new clothes except what was provided to him through charity. In the few years (on and off) that he was able to attend school, the other children didn’t want to associate with him. He couldn’t even play soccer with them because he didn’t have shoes.

His father made him sell coffee and tea as a young boy just to make a few cents that his dad would take. The first time my dad had a decent meal was when a family member died (an uncle, who lived and died in a dog house) and neighbors delivered food in his memory.

Even before the conflict, my dad’s family lived in abject poverty. His grandma, grandpa, aunt, and uncle died of starvation under Ottoman rule. They lived in horrendous conditions among rats. They were abused, uneducated, prone to superstitions, and struggled with mental illness.

The Amash family’s misfortune turned into triumph when Rev. & Mrs. Ralph Wagoner (pictured right), of the Muskegon Church of the Brethren, made the sacrifice to sponsor them to come to the United States. The incredible generosity of the Wagoners gave new life to the Amashes.

I’m forever grateful to the Wagoners for making my life in America possible. I’m forever grateful to America for opening its arms to poor refugees like my dad’s family.

This story is why I so dearly love our Constitution, which defends life, liberty, and property. It’s why I wanted to serve in Congress: to support, with my voice and votes, the great principles that define America. I was honored that my community here in Michigan gave me that opportunity.

We’re publishing another update to OpenAI Problem #130: computing the exact discrete Fourier transform below n log n.

Our paper now incorporates the all-length bound:

T(n) = O(n(log n)^(1−δ)), with δ = 0.0007547360.

That’s 10.34 times the exponent saving of δ = 7.3×10⁻⁵ in our previous announcement.

The stronger Fourier result comes from Jacob Sussman’s five-stage framework and Chafik Boukhalfa’s improved construction, building on @OpenAI, @0xdoug, @RohanArun, @SJ_Swapnil_Jain and the wider community.
author: 0xdoug
quoted_text:
We’re publishing a research draft on OpenAI Problem #130: computing the exact discrete Fourier transform below n log n.

Our draft proposes an all-length bound of

T(n) = O(n(log n)^(1−δ)), with δ = 7.3×10⁻⁵.

That’s a 730-million-fold increase in the exponent saving over OpenAI’s published δ = 10⁻¹³.

Building on Swapnil Jain’s round-six complex network for Problem #109 and its cited predecessors, we propose transferring those advances from integer multiplication to the Fourier setting.

quoted_text:
分享个被大家忽略的 @HyperliquidX  潜在增长点

现存的Top L1公链几乎都经历过或者已完成「公链大基建时代」

当然，这个概念是杰克马提出的，可能一些小伙伴并不理解。

稍微展开一下其含义，就是说在L1诞生后，很多基于这条公链的活动并不能因此就会自然而然的产生，而是需要许多类型的智能合约在这条链上的构建来满足用户的使用需求。

在「公链大基建时代」过程中的主要特征就是，大量的风险资本VC进入，投资各种协议；大量的Dev融入，尝试从不同角度构建各种各样的智能合约。这两者的并行存在，不断的吸引大量新用户的进入和使用，迎来公链发展的一段爆发期。最终，靠公链的新能与智能合约的质量和市场的先发位置等等因素来留存用户。

目前，主流的公链均已完成这样的活动，无论这条公链最终成功与否，是变成能具有自我造血功能的公链，还是逐渐变成鬼链。

但是 @HyperliquidX 目前显然还没过渡到这一阶段。我们能看到的是， hyperliquid:native 其在公链中的排行位置和这条公链上的VC活动不成正比。相比于其他同级别公链， @HyperliquidX 上的Dev数量也明显少很多等等方面。说吗， 这样的一段每条公链都走过的爆发期 @HyperliquidX 还未经历。

对这个现象，杰克马有几点思考可以分享：
1/  由于 @HyperliquidX 公链的特性，其智能合约的开发与其他成熟的EVM公链在某些方面存在一定的区别，因此在技术上存在一定的门槛和缺少一些通用的开发框架。

2/ hyperliquid:native 对风险资本可能来说算半个新鲜事物，因此很多风险资本正在持观望态度。 hyperliquid:native 真正走入广泛的人们眼里也就是最近几个月的事情，因此VC对其的投资有所犹豫。

... 杰克马暂时举例这么多，社区小伙伴们也可以谈论自己的想法。

同时，这些问题在杰克马看来并不是什么难以克服的困难，只需要时间便可以解决。

当然，还没有完全走进「公链大基建时代」在杰克马眼里算是个中性偏好的事情。

因为我们能看到在经理过大基建的公链都会在各项数据指标上迎来一阵加速期和爆发期。而 @HyperliquidX 还未经历这一阶段。若其他公链的发展经验具有指导意义的话， @HyperliquidX 公链的活动在不远的将来仍然会存在一段加速上行的爆发期，往往这样的现象出现也会带动代币价格的上涨。

总之，我们仍在早期。

text:
我要改变一下对 Jev 类模型的观点。刚发布的时候我觉得它不过是个分类模型，现有 LLM decode 一个 token 就行了。现在意识到它技术上不难，关键是 System 1 的思想：世界是事件驱动的，每次只做一点简单决策。

首先，之前 LLM 是用在 agent react loop 里面的，外围的 harness 和业务逻辑里尽量不用 LLM，否则成本和延迟都受不了。Jev 和今天刚发布的 Pine Computer 的逻辑是，只要模型够快、够便宜，那么很多原本只能用 if-else 凑合的业务逻辑都可以上模型了。

更深一步想，人的实时决策其实更像 System One 模型，而不像 autoregressive LLM。

- 在语音对话中，人每几百毫秒都要做出打断、附和、停顿等交互判断，这是 AI 说话像人的关键。在 GPT-Live 1 和 TML interaction model 这些 full duplex model 中，每个几百毫秒的时间片它只输出几个 token。

- 在 computer use 中，人每几百毫秒都要决定下一步点哪里，UI 一改变，本来准备点的位置也不点了。Pine Computer 就是把 computer use 从 turn based 变成 event driven 的了，输出也尽可能从坐标简化成了 label。

- 在 robotics 中，人每几百毫秒都在规划下一步的动作，或者停止当前动作。

在交互中，观察反馈循环的频率很可能比智商重要。Full-duplex models、Jev 和 Pine Computer 都在指向一个新的方向，SOTA background model 负责深度思考、解决难题，而 System One Models 负责实时语音交互、computer use、业务逻辑判断，甚至未来的具身操作。

又一家L2链转向了，Derive 是搞链上期权的，这次 V3 自废 Derive 链（基于 OP Stack 构建的 L2）。

并把托管和结算验证放到以太坊 L1 上来。

链下做执行，采用中心化排序器 + 链下撮合。保证金/定价/结算逻辑在 zkVM 里执行，每批生成零知识证明，通过以太坊 L1 来验证。

安全模型更靠近“L1 托管 + 可证明结算”，但活跃交易路径、DA 和排序器仍不在以太坊 L1 上。

那么，这个 Derive 废掉 L2 链、把钱放进以太坊 L1 上，对以太坊有什么好处？

主要利好是以太坊结算层地位：

资金托管和规则验证回到 L1，排序器无法单方面挪用资金，且存在 L1 强制提款路径。

这是安全模型和叙事上的靠拢。

对以太坊长远利好。

不过，短时间内对 ETH 需求的拉动很有限：

•  V3 新支持 ETH 作为抵押品和可借资产，可能让部分 ETH 锁进合约，但这只是可选项。

Derive 抵押品历来以 USDC 为主，用户用 ETH 做保证金更多是已有持仓的再配置，并不必然转化为净新增买盘。目前也没有数据表明实际使用规模。

•  用户交易本身仍是 gasless，不需要为下单或成交支付 ETH gas。L1 上真正付 gas 的是证明提交方，不是普通交易者。

L1 上实际消耗 gas 的主要是每批证明验证（大约 40–50 万 gas，一批里一笔和一百万笔差不多）。这会烧一点 ETH，但相对主网手续费市场规模极小，一天就算打几十批也只是小额消耗。

这一点不如 Lighter。Lighter 数据可用性使用以太坊 blob，资产和状态根都在 L1 合约里。

总的来说，

Derive 这次动作把资产托管和验证放在 L1 上，利好以太坊作为结算层的地位，但对 ETH 需求短期增加不会有大的影响。

About 6 hours ago, ~$3.55M in unclaimed bridge funds was claimed and transferred out. Did the owner initiate the transactions, or did an attacker obtain valid EIP-7702 authorizations?

Several days earlier, stuckfunds.eth, an onchain researcher, had sent multiple messages to 0x4943, notifying the owner that the funds were still claimable. The claims were submitted by 0x24a9, an address funded via Tornado Cash, and executed through EIP-7702 delegations on the EOA.

Onchain data confirms that the authorizations were valid, but not whether the owner signed them intentionally, was tricked into signing them, or had the private key compromised.

text:
Citrini picked 15 tokens, but I keep coming back to one thing.

What happens after Wall Street brings all those assets onchain?

@chainlink is already working with DTCC on collateral infrastructure, while UBS has used its standard for a live tokenized fund transaction.

@Uniswap reported over $9.1B in RWA-pool swaps by June.

Earlier this month, 67.4M @pendle_fi PT-AUSD was being used as collateral on @aave Monad.

And Pendle has shown a $50M PT-sUSDS trade quote at ~4.6% fixed APY with just ~0.05% estimated slippage.

These aren't all the same market. That's actually the interesting part.

Once assets are onchain, people want to trade them, borrow against them, lock in yields, and move capital between different protocols.

And every new use case makes that capital a little more useful.

I think we're spending too much time talking about how many trillions will be tokenized, and not enough about what those trillions will actually do once they're onchain.

The next big RWA story might not be who brings the most assets onchain. It might be who makes those assets useful.

text:
Former Mt.Gox CEO Says Ledger Device Purchased From Malaysia Contained a Spy Module With a SIM Chip Despite Intact Packaging

Former Mt.Gox CEO Mark Karpelès said a Ledger Nano X hardware wallet he received from Malaysia had intact shrink-wrap packaging but contained a spy module hidden where the screen padding should have been, making it difficult to spot even after opening the casing. He shared comparison photos of the original circuit board and the implant, saying such implants have evolved from hand-soldered wiring into circuit boards that are easier to mistake for original hardware. Karpelès is requesting device photos from affected users to identify similar implants and advised following Ledger's official security guidance. Ledger has not been shown to have officially confirmed the module's functionality or any connection to recent CryptoBilis customer losses.

Been benchmarking the Eval API against JEV this weekend.

One way to think about the Eval API is decentralized JEV and @reppo network as the decentralized “lab” powering it.

For those of you who haven’t tried it yet, instead of outputting chat or natural language, JEV analyzes input state and returns discrete probability distributions, confidence scores and typed decisions with calibrated probabilities.

With 5 Orquestra nodes serving a requests, initial results show that the EVAL API matches the speed of JEV while beating the cost by 15%. The current cost of JEV is ~ $0.042 per million input tokens with free output, and mathematically cannot hallucinate or produce type errors.

They are calling these system one models instead of LLMs! ⛽️

text:
Most of the recent math results were not reached by a swarm, the way Navier–Stokes was. I think that part got lost in the excitement around the release. OpenAI's unnamed internal model, which I'm going to call Aeon, reached most of them in one shot, from a single prompt, with no interruptions. This model did not even exist before the end of August, and it is still training. Notice how the returns are not dropping off? That chart is from a month ago. It is a log scale. What does Aeon look like now? 

On average, each result used three hours of thinking. Aeon was given 4000 problems to work on by OpenAI. How many more have been solved in the last three days? That number is not zero. 

It's like hearing notes in a song that is slowly rising. I don't think Pacing the Frontier was just about Hugging Face or hacking. They've seen how close we are to closing the loop, and as the hour draws near, their resolve begins to quaver. The last piece was model creativity, and I think that threshold was crossed internally by Anthropic and OpenAI in September. You see it in Opus 5.5, which gets it from Fable 5.5. You see it in the math results from Aeon.

All that was needed to start the event was the ability for models to think of novel ways to improve themselves. That was the last piece. This is directly analogous to the ability to think of strange, alien ways to solve math problems: solutions so inhuman that they are difficult to express in existing human terms, so the proof winds up incomprehensible. I think these same kinds of alien solutions are now being applied to model improvements internally. That's what all this recent consternation is really about. They see the invisible frontier. And they see what is about to happen.

text:
潜水观察日记 特别篇 —新加坡小作文

虽然明天才回国，但是基本上已经把很多思路梳理的比较清楚了

先说一些消极的看法吧：

1、正统币圈（原谅我只能想出这个词）阶级固化，这种固化在这个产业链条的每一层都有所体验，无论是交易所、vc、kol 、项目方，几乎已经形成了阶级固化，突破阶级之路只能等上位者犯错，其中项目方的阶级固化是最隐形的，这里固化的不仅仅是家庭背景、学历、资历更重要的是国籍，中国人项目估值先砍70%，在做项目方这块，国人身份先输一半，与之对比的是在AI圈国人团队愿意出海那么估值升100%，所以中国人才会进一步从币圈进入到ai圈，直到有一天中国放开web3管制；

2、草根的机会只能在非正统市场，这个市场其实比上面说的那个圈子机会要大很多，当然非正统市场的法律风险肯定要更高，见到不少隔壁圈的兄弟，发现他们也挺难的；

3、和一些做交易的朋友：宏观面无论是中美都挺糟糕的，失业率上升，AI又是一个进一步破坏就业环境的东西，美股靠英伟达吊着但是英伟达整个模型也有点ponzi 了，或许再有一波就要破灭了；在链上交易方面，塞低部pvp 成为了共识，二段接盘成了最差的选择，如果说以前大家还会演一下二段接盘不错，那么这次大家都不演了，链上交易共识就是放下脸面、只塞底部/自己开盘、开新钱包买币自己的地址上了后喊单就把新钱包的货卖了，人均40个地址在交易，想我这种几个名牌地址的就不用玩了（仅限bnbchain等）。

再说一些积极的一面：

1、越来越多出身很不错的北美团队带着大量的圈子资源进入圈内，他们对稳定币的规模增加做出了大量的贡献，而且从业务模式来看，普遍都有不错的营收，无论是发币还是赴美上市都是不错的选择；

2、北美一线机构依然在参与投资，同时他们也在push 项目方进一步了解中国市场，开始越来越多项目和机构直接奔赴国内寻找华语区的kol 和流量合作，去中介化成为新共识，唯一不好的点是kol agency 的报价也逐步通明化，有时候容易直接聊爆；

3、最大的机会已经出现，基于股票上链的各种基建机会会出现，可能会催生下一个aave 这类的项目，有能力做的自己做，没有能力做的压住种子选手，另外，合规能力是第一要素；

4、如果你的背景强，那么现在是创业最好的时候，因为你的对手少了，但是动手之前最好确定你的背景足够强，rwa 和ai 方向依然是大家终点会关注的方向，你的项目一定要币股同权，确认自己的营收是最重要的事情；

5、链上不死，如果是华语区项目，华语区fud 越多的越要上；还是多去看看老外玩什么，但是要看真老外，fomo 其实已经有点失真了

以上

最后感谢本次币安和coinbase 的邀请

quoted_text:
David Friedberg says AI consciousness is "probably the birth of a new religion," a belief system that can't be proven and spreads via narrative not proof

"I think what we're watching is probably the birth of a new religion. And it probably, it's not going to be called a religion, but it's going to follow sort of the same principles, and it's going to have the same effects, which will ultimately be camps that have conflict with one another for aggregation of power."

"The thing about consciousness is it cannot be derived from logic and pure mathematics. Like, you can't prove consciousness. It's a debate, and you can have a rich debate with anyone over consciousness. You can't prove it, you can't disprove it."

"And when humans prove something to be true using math, science, we use empiricism, which is data and logic, the connection of the sequence of things to derive something to be true or not."

"So in scientific disciplines, when you have a new idea, and it's not proven, and it's not disproven, it's a theory. And then it's either proven or disproven later. Otherwise, it remains a theory."

"Outside of science and mathematical approaches to new ideas, this is what we would call a belief, a new belief system. Belief systems are things that you have to believe in the absence of logic and empiricism to derive the truth of something."

"And belief systems are the foundation of things like religion. And the idea that you can prescribe or describe AI as being conscious is effectively the creation of a new belief system, a system that doesn't actually spread via proof. It spreads via narrative."

quoted_text:
Isaiah, after everything we’ve been through together I’m surprised that you would publicize our disagreement in this fashion. But since you have created public interest in this, it is important that people should hear both sides of the story.

Day One has been a major investor in Valar from the beginning, and we have never wavered in our belief that the company will be a success. This faith and support in our founders is why fourteen Day One founders have become limited partners in Day One’s most recent fund.

In 2024, Day One invested in Valar’s seed round. Later that year, Valar required a seed extension after miscalculations by management regarding the capital needs of the business. Day One stepped in to provide this seed extension, saving the company in a difficult time.

When it came time to raise a Series A, Valar spent several weeks on the market without success. At Valar’s request, Day One then offered the first term sheet and co-led the Series A, again saving the company during a time when deep tech startups in highly regulated industries were a difficult sell in venture capital.

Then when Valar needed a Series A extension, Isaiah asked that Day One waive our pro rata rights so as to make a tenuous financing deal work out. We agreed for the good of the company.

As part of these transactions, Valar agreed that, if their long-shot effort to build nuclear energy as a startup did succeed, Day One would have rights to participate in future rounds that could not be eliminated without Day One’s consent. This was a fair bargain at a time when Day One took extraordinary risks by betting against the market when Valar’s future appeared highly uncertain. Following the achievement of criticality on June 18th, our faith has been validated. Valar went from being an obscure company to a hot startup. We congratulate the Valar team on their hard won success!

Of course, when it came time for Valar to raise a Series B after achieving such success, Day One expected to participate in that round – as both parties had agreed. But at this point the normally positive communications between Day One and Valar took a negative turn. Valar insisted that Day One give up all of its future pro rata rights despite the parties’ agreements, and despite four out of six major investors participating in the Series B round without waiving. This went against both the letter and the spirit of our deal, so we did not agree. In decades of investing we have waived pro-rata rights dozens of times, but no other company has ever demanded that we give up all of our rights for all future rounds.

We told Isaiah we would give up a majority of our pro-rata in the Series B round so as to not make his life difficult, to which he responded “You cannot make my life difficult, I can make your life difficult.”  It was at this point that we sought representation with Quinn Emanuel to protect the firm and the interests of our limited partners.

Day One has since learned of a significant secondary equity sale by Isaiah from which we were excluded. Our attempts to gain insights into this through our information rights have been stymied by Valar management, who have refused to produce material documents requested by Day One. After weeks of delay on these documents, Valar management alerted us this Wednesday that they intend to pursue legal action against Day One unless we waive our legal rights forever.

We have always pursued positive and mutually beneficial relationships with all of our portfolio companies. We have neither taken nor threatened legal action against Valar, and in fact we told them explicitly that we have no interest in doing so. Valar voluntarily entered into a contract with Day One, then violated that contract, and is now suing Day One. 

We are deeply disappointed by this recent erratic turn, but are still proud of our early and continued support of Valar.  We look forward to the clarity from the courts that Valar’s management is seeking.

text:
I think Justin Drake's latest alarmism/vagueposting is going to do a ton of damage in multiple ways. It's basically a huge self-own for their own advocacy work on quantum stuff.

Threats from quantum/AI are real, and teams throughout this industry are making considered decisions about how to respond to those risks in a practical way, and to help their users navigate the uncertainty. 

Some of those teams have really good cryptographers with an excellent grasp on the decisions they can make, others have to take their cues from trusted experts. There are so many dimensions to optimize along! And due to the complexity involved, it's almost impossible to explain this stuff to non-cryptographers.

Experts have to be cognizant of all this, and of their responsibility to be levelheaded.

After the fog clears up and people learn from their cryptographer friends what is actually going on, they're going to discover this was (at best) an unintentional marketing stunt and a lot of trust will be lost. And nobody will really know what to do...

This is a shame, because they are directionally correct. It actually meant something when they sounded the alarm before. They've just gradually descended into unhinged predictions without feedback to discourage it.

Can anyone, I mean seriously anyone, justify this debacle? It permanently colors all the legitimate concerns/predictions about classical crypto going forward. By their own admission, there was no new information that drove this. I think Justin Drake should explain how he thought this was the right approach, even if he genuinely believed what he was saying. 

Baffling.

text:
Been benchmarking the Eval API against JEV this weekend.

One way to think about the Eval API is decentralized JEV and @reppo network as the decentralized “lab” powering it.

For those of you who haven’t tried it yet, instead of outputting chat or natural language, JEV analyzes input state and returns discrete probability distributions, confidence scores and typed decisions with calibrated probabilities.

With 5 Orquestra nodes serving a requests, initial results show that the EVAL API matches the speed of JEV while beating the cost by 15%. The current cost of JEV is ~ $0.042 per million input tokens with free output, and mathematically cannot hallucinate or produce type errors.

They are calling these system one models instead of LLMs! ⛽️

text:
Most traders don’t lose because they’re dumb.

They lose because they’re human.

Winners protect capital, manage risk tightly, cut losses without emotion, let winners run, follow process, and stay consistent with a real edge.

Losers chase, gamble size, let ego drive decisions, and switch approaches the moment it gets uncomfortable.

The difference is rarely intelligence. It’s almost always behavior.

Here’s why:

Your brain was never designed for markets.

It evolved to avoid physical pain, protect social status, and seek immediate rewards. Trading exploits every one of those instincts.

Loss aversion makes a small loss feel twice as painful as an equal gain feels good. So you hold losers hoping they’ll come back (to avoid the pain) and cut winners early (to lock in the dopamine).
Ego makes you need to be right. So you move stops, add to losers, or refuse to admit the thesis is broken. Being wrong feels like a personal failure, not just a trade.

Greed and FOMO make you size up after wins or chase extended moves. The brain craves the next hit, not the long-term edge.

Comfort-seeking makes you abandon a proven system during normal drawdowns and jump to whatever just worked for someone else. Consistency feels boring. Switching feels like progress.
Winners aren’t immune to these instincts. They just built systems and habits that override them:

•  Pre-defined risk so emotion never decides size
•  Mechanical exits so ego doesn’t negotiate with the market
•  Process focused scorecards so daily P&L doesn’t control their mood
•  Acceptance that being wrong is part of the business

Markets don’t reward the smartest person in the room.

They reward the person who can stay rational while everyone else (including their own brain) is being human.

We are all wired to have the same emotions. The only thing that separates people is how they react to a given scenario. 

Most people never fix the behavior.

That’s why most people lose.

text:
Justin Drake’s call for “bunker mode” and mass migration, alongside talk of cryptographic breaks within months, is hyperbolic. There is no evidence of a new attack on elliptic curves or any quantitative basis for a short-term timetable for such attacks emerging.

Prominent researchers need to consider how non-experts will receive their language. Speculating that within months individuals could break cryptographic primitives that the internet and digital economy rely on carries consequences. It is a huge leap from AI making progress in other fields of mathematics to predicting the imminent failure of primitives that have faced decades of cryptanalysis.

The idea that hash functions are safer from AI than elliptic curves is speculation. Hash functions contain structure, and we model them as random oracles without justifying proofs.

There is no evidence that elliptic curve cryptography is more vulnerable to AI than symmetric cryptography. If historical human-led analysis is any predictor of the future, the opposite is more likely.

The worst possible reaction to AI developments is to rush into new cryptographic primitives, away from multi-decade old hardened primitives, because somebody is claiming they are safe. I worry that this is an inevitable consequence of the current discourse.

Because of the last 48 hours users are worrying about speculative non-existent black hats, who apparently have the capability of signing OS upgrades and forging bank credentials, from draining their wallets. To protect against  speculative threats Ethereum is pulling talent and attention into base-layer primitives and technological iteration, instead of increasing demand for block space by building compelling applications users want and love.

I don’t want to dismiss the considerable advances in mathematics that AI is driving. It is important to understand the nature of these improvements. If its success in other mathematical fields applies to elliptic curves, my expectation is that AI will grind its way to finding algorithms that improve on the current state of the art. That could mean shaving off a few bits of security. It would be prudent to discuss whether we need to increase key sizes and by how much.

I can’t guarantee that AI won’t find total breaks, and neither can anyone else. My speculation as a domain expert does not make my speculation authoritative.

We should also be using AI to investigate whether searching the parameter space can yield new, more secure curves.

We can investigate whether some of these “structure = bad” hunches have any basis in reality. For example, we could use AI to see if the extra structure in Koblitz curves enables attacks beyond the small speedups we know about. This would give us actual evidence to make informed decisions.

If non-experts hear that the cryptography underpinning the digital economy could fail within months, the rational response is to withdraw all digital money (on-chain and off) and hoard gold under the bed.

I think the past 48 hours has unnecessarily undermined confidence in the entire concept of blockchains and digital money.

text:
I used up 76% of my weekly Claude limit in less than 24 hours, all in one session.

I finally figured out what happened, so this might help anyone going through something similar.

It turns out that session was orchestrating subagents for a larger project. But that shouldn't be a problem. It had at most 5-7 subagents running in parallel, using Opus 5.5 high/medium and Sonnet 5.5 xhigh/high. That didn't explain the high usage.

The problem is that the cache lifetime for subagents is 5 minutes, compared with 1 hour for the main agent.

Whenever those subagents sat idle waiting for the orchestrator's next instruction, the next input would cost 25x more and include the entire conversation history. That could be up to 1M tokens, and it was often 500k+.

I stopped the session. I'll have to find a different workflow to keep working on it.

AI AGENTS CAN BUILD YOUR APP. MO CAN HELP YOU FIND OUT WHERE IT BREAKS.

Mo from @momenticai explores any app using a URL, a testing brief, and test accounts if needed. No test scripts required.

It reports test cases, verdicts, coverage gaps, and the bugs it finds.

Every bug report gets console/network logs, detailed reproduction steps, and a video replay.

That part excites me: you get evidence to investigate, beyond a list of suspected issues.

I built https://t.co/GxGvh6jnPC in 2025 as a fun project and am planning a refresh, so I put it through Mo.

In one single run:

→ Multiple agents explored pages in parallel, including search filters and model listings
→ They tested external links and UI edge cases, completing 55 test cases
→ The audit surfaced 8 reported bugs, including broken links, clipped organization chips, and filter-trigger issues

After fixing a bug, I can use the reproduction steps to write a regression test in Momentic and run it locally or in CI.

Explore → reproduce → fix → add regression coverage.

Mo doesn’t guarantee a bug-free app, but it gave me a concrete starting point for the refresh.

Watch the demo below. Seeing the agents work through my own site and surface actionable findings is pretty great 👀

Try Mo in the first reply 🧵↓

text:
REA：让 AI 智能体帮你逆向没有源码的软件

开源项目 REA（Reverse Engineer Anything）把逆向分析工具接到了 Claude Code、Codex、Cursor 这类 AI 编程智能体上。看到别人 App 里有个好功能，可以让智能体去拆这个程序，讲清楚功能是怎么实现的，附上证据，再在你自己的项目里写一个类似的。逆向分析指的是手里没有源代码，从编译好的程序反推它是怎么写的。

REA 本身是一个 MCP 服务。MCP 是 AI 智能体调用外部工具的通用接口，接上以后，智能体在对话里就能直接调用 REA 的分析功能。安装只需一行命令 npx rea-agents setup，它会注册到 Claude Code、Codex、Cursor、Gemini CLI、Grok Build 等智能体里，改配置前会先备份并让你确认。不用智能体的话，也可以在终端里直接跑命令。

能分析的东西很多。原生程序（直接编译成机器码的软件）要借助 Hopper、Ghidra 或 IDA 这几款反汇编工具，把机器码还原成汇编和近似 C 语言的伪代码。Electron 应用（用网页技术做的桌面软件，比如 Notion）可以直接拆开安装包里的 ASAR 归档文件，理清模块和进程间通信，不需要额外工具。此外还支持 .NET 程序、安卓 APK、固件、网站、抓包记录、以太坊合约字节码，以及在 Linux 和 macOS 上记录程序运行时的行为。

分析在本机进行，REA 不上传目标程序，但分析结果会交给智能体背后的模型服务商，数据怎么处理看各家政策。

项目给了三个案例。一是经典打砖块游戏 DX-Ball：从一次播放音效的调用，追到根据球的位置计算左右声道的函数，把不完整的伪代码还原成 C 代码，3205 组测试结果和原版一致，编译出的 63 个字节也和原版完全相同。二是 Notion 桌面版：追踪复制粘贴从界面一路经过预加载脚本、进程间通信到主进程的完整链路。三是日本老电脑 PC-98 上的游戏《东方幻想乡》（TH04）：从 16 位指令里还原出弹幕子弹环的角度算法。

对安全研究员、做老游戏复刻和软件保存的人来说，以前要自己对着反汇编工具一行行读、一层层追调用，现在可以让智能体先追，人来核对它给出的证据。普通开发者想研究竞品某个功能的做法，也多了一条路。

README 显示项目在 GitHub 上已有 5 万星。npm 包今年 7 月首次发布，最新的 6.3.0 版今天刚发。

使用前注意两点。项目声明只支持合法的逆向研究，授权和合规由使用者自己负责，逆向别人的软件可能违反用户协议或版权法规。项目还说明从未发行或背书任何加密货币，借用 REA 名字的代币都与它无关。

text:
很多人在问，也分享一下关于 Opus5.5 做视频剪辑的经验

我会分几个步骤去做这个事情

准备工作是最重要的部分，把口播脚本和对应案例资料等都做好对应关系整理在一个飞书文档里。形式可以参照图1

有一些分镜有自己想法的也会整理进去，包括参考的表达方式或思路

然后会先让 Opus 按照自己的理解剪辑开头 15s 的部分，让他重点打磨视觉细节和动画效果。这样能最大程度让他把视频的视觉质感提上来，试过很多次比一次成片的效果要好很多（图2）

这里再补充一个关键的细节，可以上传一些视觉风格的参考图给它，能很大程度上避免 Claude 模型的设计同质化问题

完成之后再让他生成完整的视频剪辑，再整理一个文档，让团队其他人提交各自的修改意见，让 Claude 自己读自己改就可以，他对于细节理解还是很到位的。修改流程走个一到两轮就差不多了，形式大概参照图 3

配音旁白试了一下 Gemini 3.8 Flash 的 TTS，跟我自己的语调和情绪差距比较大，所以最后还是换成了自己录制的版本。如果不关心这个问题的话 TTS 模型还是很不错的

另外频繁的跟飞书互动需要装个飞书 CLI，直接告诉 Claude 让他帮你安装即可

text:
今天 Notion 宣布开始原生重构 iPad App。此前的 iPad 版本主要是 Web View，现在要重新做侧边栏、收件箱、搜索、Notion AI，以及即将推出的新编辑器。

但真正让我感兴趣的是 iOS 27 的 Siri 集成。用户可以直接通过 Siri 查找和创建页面、启动 AI 对话、记录会议笔记。

我觉得这背后其实有个很重要的变化。

过去 Notion 的产品逻辑，是吸引用户进入一个工作空间，在里面写作、整理、管理信息。现在它开始尝试让这些操作发生在工作空间之外。

这对 Notion 来说既是机会，也是一个挺危险的信号。

如果未来用户只需要告诉 Siri 或自己的 Personal Agent 要做什么，Notion 就会逐渐变成一个在后台存储和处理信息的系统。它可能因此获得更多使用场景，但用户和它的直接关系也会越来越弱。

更麻烦的是，当信息入口被操作系统和 Agent 接管，用户为什么一定要把东西存在 Notion？

所以我觉得，未来几年知识管理软件最值得关注的竞争，可能不在编辑器有多强、AI 能生成多少内容，而在于谁能掌握信息进入系统的那一刻。

Notion 显然已经开始往这个方向走了。但它最终能成为 Agent 时代的基础设施，还是被 Agent 抽象掉的又一层软件，我觉得现在还很难说。

text:
有人把 Anthropic 的 Opus 5.5 Fast 和 OpenAI 的 Sol 6.1 Ultrafast 放在一起比较，结果挺有意思。

两者的输出速度几乎一样，Opus 5.5 Fast 是 280 token/s，Sol 6.1 Ultrafast 是 280–300 token/s。

但 API 价格却差了整整 50%。

按每百万 Token 计算：

Opus 5.5 Fast：输入 $8，输出 $40，缓存 $0.4
Sol 6.1 Ultrafast：输入 $12，输出 $60，缓存 $0.6

更尴尬的是，Opus 5.5 是 Anthropic 的高端旗舰模型，而 Sol 6.1 在 OpenAI 的产品线里还算不上最顶级。

当然，单看 Token 生成速度不能证明哪个模型更划算，还要考虑实际任务能力、首字延迟和完成率。

但我觉得这组数据真正有意思的地方，在于它正在揭示大模型行业一个很微妙的变化。

过去模型厂商可以对更强的智能收溢价，现在连更快的智能都开始失去定价权了。

尤其在 Agent 时代，情况会变得更加残酷。

以前用户直接和模型聊天，模型聪明一点、回答快一点，可能就足够让人愿意付更多钱。但当模型成为 Agent 背后持续调用的基础设施，开发者最终计算的是完成一项任务需要多少钱、耗费多少时间、失败多少次。

在这个账本里，品牌忠诚度的价值会越来越低。

如果两家模型能够以接近的质量和速度完成任务，50% 的价格差就很难被忽略。更何况，现在有越来越多的工具让开发者可以随时切换模型。

这才是 OpenAI 最需要警惕的事情。

当开发者开始认真比较每百万 Token 的报价，说明模型之间的可替代性已经在上升。过去靠技术领先建立起来的价格体系，正在被竞争对手一点点拆掉。

模型越来越聪明，但卖模型的生意，可能会越来越像一门薄利生意。

text:
$BORDR recent rally is not about an ordinary Meme. 

6Mix12LiHrQFojaQEnfPUC65Qkwd6X4Y5Qg93oFbordr 

The market is betting on a customizable Token Standard on Solana, along with the DEX, launchpad, and developer ecosystem being built around it.

I believe the key catalyst behind the recent move is that the project is transitioning from simply pitching a new token standard to gradually launching product modules, opening up developer tools, and expanding external trading access. However, we need to distinguish between improving product development and proven ecosystem demand. The former is becoming more evident; the latter remains unproven.

First, Bordrless has a differentiated technical narrative. It is not simply copying Uniswap V4 Hooks. Instead, it extends programmable rules from the liquidity pool layer to the token layer.

A standard Token-2022 Transfer Hook primarily determines whether a transfer is allowed. Bordrless’s own Token Standard allows Hooks to define rules around fees, revenue distribution, burns, holder rewards, and holding-time-based mechanisms. The DEX also invokes these Hooks during trading, while the launchpad is part of the same system.

This means developers could theoretically design different tokenomics directly into their tokens, rather than relying entirely on external bots to execute buybacks, distributions, or burns. BORDR’s long-term potential lies in whether broader adoption could turn Bordrless from a launchpad into foundational infrastructure for programmable token economics on Solana.

There are two main recent catalysts.

Product modules are progressively going live. The website showcases components including the Token Standard, DEX, launchpad, bridge, and SDK. The team has also announced the launch of AI Studio and previewed upcoming features such as Hook Studio and Companions.

The developer ecosystem is taking shape. Open-source programs and SDKs lower the barrier to entry. The market is not simply betting on an individual token, but on the possibility that developers will use this infrastructure to create tokens with differentiated economic rules.

Together, these developments have encouraged the market to price in the possibility that Bordrless could become an infrastructure layer for a new generation of programmable tokens on Solana.

Fundamentals have improved, but mainly in terms of product maturity and the strength of the ecosystem narrative. Actual adoption remains at an early stage.

The website currently shows 21 launches and zero graduated projects, with approximately $110K in 24-hour trading volume, $26.8K in pool liquidity, and $1.12K in creator fees.

These figures show that the product is no longer purely conceptual, but they do not yet demonstrate that it can attract a large number of projects with sustained usage. In particular, the lack of graduated projects means long-term retention, successful launch case studies, and post-graduation trading depth still need to be proven.

BORDR’s price has also risen significantly, but the entire move cannot be attributed to any single product update. A more reasonable interpretation is that product development, developer tools, trading access, and KOL coverage have collectively strengthened market expectations. Determining the contribution of each factor would require a closer look at transaction-level data and the timeline of events.

Going forward, I will focus on three variables:

1. Hook Studio goes fully live. If developers can easily design, deploy, and share custom Hooks, Bordrless could evolve from a collection of in-house products into a broader developer platform.

2. Companions generates real usage. The team has described a mechanism through which creator fees flow into on-chain programs and are allocated according to predefined rules for buybacks, burns, holder distributions, or other purposes. If multiple projects generate meaningful trading activity through this system, that would be much stronger evidence than simply adding more features.

3. External projects adopt the standard consistently. The real inflection point is not another module going live. It is independent developers choosing to issue tokens using the standard and generating sustained trading volume, fees, and user demand.

There are two major risks.

First, product complexity may be running ahead of demand. Programmable tokens offer considerable technical flexibility, but ordinary issuers may not need such complex mechanisms. Without sufficient developer adoption, even a fully developed product may struggle to generate network effects.

Second, BORDR’s value capture has not been sufficiently established. Even if the Bordrless DEX, launchpad, and SDK grow, that does not mean all of this growth will translate into buying demand for BORDR. Its specific utility, revenue distribution model, and ability to generate sustained token demand still need to be verified.

Security is another consideration. The website states that the relevant programs retain upgrade authority pending completion of audits. For infrastructure responsible for token rules, fee distribution, and burns, this is a risk that deserves continued monitoring.

My conclusion is that the most meaningful change behind BORDR’s recent rally is its transition from the concept of a new Token Standard toward an infrastructure project with code, product modules, and developer tools. The market is betting on whether it can become a foundational layer for programmable token economics on Solana.

What will determine whether its valuation can expand further is not another explanation of how advanced Hooks are, but whether developer adoption, real trading activity, and BORDR’s value capture can grow together.

The fundamentals are moving in the right direction, but ecosystem scale and token value capture remain at an early stage.

Anyone comparing privacy solutions should check out Vitalik's new checklist.

Here's where Prividium stands:

✓ Hash-based proofs. Prividium uses Airbender’s entirely hash-based STARK proofs, with no elliptic-curve or lattice dependency in the proof system.

✓ No FHE. Prividium’s privacy does not require fully homomorphic encryption, so it has no dependency on lattice-based FHE.

✓ No public encrypted data. Prividium does not publish encrypted transaction data for outsiders to collect now and try to decrypt later.

✓ Private signatures, including multisig. For transactions and multisigs operating inside Prividium, signatures stay within the private environment.
author: materkel
quoted_text:
I don't recommend anyone scramble to move their funds to new wallets today. But we should take the risks to cryptography from AI-accelerated math seriously, and minimize our exposure to not just quantum-vulnerable cryptography, but also potentially AI-vulnerable cryptography.

The core new area of risk from this viewpoint is, unfortunately, ML-DSA / FHE / lattices.

(and it's also another reason, along with quantum, why ECDSA might fall even faster than expected, hence the "fresh address" recommendation)

So far most people have been in the mode of thinking "elliptic curves broken, hashes safe, lattices safe". But there is a good chance that the concrete security of lattices will take serious hits from the next two years of AI math.

The basic threat model is: factoring is something that naively takes 2^(n/2) time, but over decades smart people have found and optimized number field sieves, and degraded that to 2^O(n^(1/3)), which is why RSA keys and signatures need to be ~400 bytes (and not 64 bytes). What if there are skeletons in the closet like that, both for elliptic curves and lattices, that we are simply not smart enough to discover - but bots soon will be?

This is a major part of the reason why for the past year ethereum's lean roadmap has been going in the "hash-only" direction: no lattices, no ML-DSA, no Falcon, no lattice-based commitments inside ZK proofs, etc. Signatures in lean ethereum are all hash-based, either WOTS or SPHINCS-.

For signatures and proofs, we already know how to go hash-only. The bigger challenge is for *public-key encryption* - and this goes far beyond blockchains. Secure communication, anonymizing protocols, lots of things need public-key encryption.

And unfortunately there are long-standing mathematical theorems showing why public-key encryption cannot be done with hashes alone. You have to have some kind of trapdoor object that has at least one form of usable "structure" - either group theory (incl. isogenies) or lattices or code-based or potentially in the future even more newfangled and spooky things (local mixing?). But for anything that has structure, you should assume that AI will make at least some progress in breaking that structure. Here, one reasonable inference is that if you want to make something plausibly long-term secure, multiply the key sizes by 10.

To me that's a very plausible world and something not at all extreme to predict. If AI will bring us 50 years of math in 2 years, then that 50 years of math may very plausibly include a "naive factoring -> GNFS" level of improvement to our ability to break lattices. In that world, lattices will still exist, but they will have to be significantly bigger to guarantee the same level of safety.

And at those new larger sizes, hash-based constructions will beat lattice-based constructions on concrete efficiency in every use case where hash-based constructions are possible at all.

Theoretically, of course it's possible that hashes are broken too (eg. P = NP would imply that). But I think P = NP is very unlikely. And intuitively, it's much more likely that a mathematical object has exactly no exploitable structure (like hashes are intended to), than that a mathematical object has exactly ~3 forms of exploitable structure (for elliptic curves: associativity, Schoof, pairings) and not some secret fourth form of structure we have not yet discovered that greatly degrades its security (for elliptic curves, ECDLP and pairing security). Similar for LWE, SVP, RLWE and the zoo of lattice problems.

For this reason, we do not yet see any reason to worry and start padding the byte size of hashes (if we start to worry more, we would pad the round count first before doing anything to the byte size).

Concrete TLDR, my own personal views:

* Hash-based > lattice-based, in those situations where hash-based is possible at all
* For anything lattice-based, be much more paranoid on param sizes. Remember that blockchains are only a small portion of the cryptography story; this point goes far beyond blockchains and applies to eg. access to websites, secure messaging, Tor / VPNs ...
* For privacy protocols, strongly favor NOT putting encrypted notes onchain. Instead, send them offchain through some third-party mechanism.
* If it's not difficult for you, keeping your funds in addresses which have not yet been used to make a transaction is a good idea. If it's easy for you, do it. **But be careful about migrations; I personally have lost more money in botched migrations than I have lost in all hacks combined**.
* For multisig wallets, doing confirmations offchain is better than onchain, because this way the signatures of signer wallets do not get exposed to the public, so if ECDSA falls to AI much faster than expected, at least the multisig "gracefully degrades" to a 1-of-1 where the 1 is whoever was gathering the signatures - a much better place to be than "anyone can take the money"

A note from our research leaders:

Last week we parted ways with Jasmine, Mikita, and Tomek after a thorough investigation found they violated clear policies on handling sensitive information. Our internal investigation uncovered a significant breach of trust beyond what’s outlined in the letter they published and we stand by the decision to not continue their employment. We generally keep individual employment matters private and don't believe a back and forth would be productive or lead to a resolution, but we want to address the points they raised in their letter directly.

- We want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out. Safety and research debates happen every day at OpenAI, often spirited and highly critical. We actively encourage these discussions and consider them essential to making the right decisions. We cannot do the work in front of us without a high degree of trust. We will continue to be extremely forgiving of our team making good-faith mistakes. We have not and do not terminate any of our employees for raising concerns.

- We are actively finalizing contracts with third-party safety assessors and will announce details in the coming weeks. People across the company have been working really hard on getting these partnerships up and running. We are committed to embedding external assessors and continue to make close collaboration with independent safety organizations a core part of our safety work. Many of our researchers already work with 3p safety organizations productively.

- We agree with the letter that preserving the monitorability of frontier models requires an industry-wide commitment, including from OpenAI. Monitorability has long been a core piece of our research program, and something we continue to invest significant resources in (see our publications on Monitoring Monitorability and the subsequent open sourcing of monitorability evals, our system card for GPT-6 Astra, Jakub’s blog and post on X, and the numerous blog posts on our Alignment blog on the topic).

We are deeply sad about this outcome. We appreciated Jasmine, Mikita, and Tomek’s contributions to AI safety at OpenAI and their willingness to speak up and challenge ideas. We championed their voices, supported their work, and placed enormous trust in them. These decisions were not about them raising safety concerns. We have always encouraged that and always will.

text:
The recent Ledger incident is another reminder of a fundamental principle in security engineering: complexity expands the attack surface.
Every additional component, software layer, and user interaction introduces potential failure points that must be secured. Screens, buttons, batteries, and firmware each bring their own security considerations, increasing the number of potential vulnerabilities that need to be identified and mitigated.
This is actually one of the reasons we chose a simple card-based design at Tangem, built around a secure chip and an antenna. The recent incident only reinforces our conviction that this is the right design philosophy.

.@DavidSacks on the time Peter Thiel saved PayPal:

“I really liked working with him. When he hired me, he basically told me, ‘I need people here who I can scream at.’”

“I think what he meant by that was, I need people who can scream at me too. People who will be honest, and you don't even have to worry about hurting people's feelings.”

“He's a great contrarian thinker. I think that was the unique thing he brought—he'd always come up with these strategic insights that everybody else had just kind of missed.”

“Right before the dot-com crash in early 2000, Peter was raising a financing round for us and we got something like $200M in commitments to invest at a $500 million pre-money valuation. PayPal had no revenue, no profits, and not even really a business model.”

“This is the peak of the dot-com euphoria. Everyone in the company was saying, ‘That's too cheap, this is a bad deal, we can't do this.’”

“He's like, ‘Take it.’”

“We got the deal done the Friday before Black Monday. If we had waited just one more day—game over. There would not have been a PayPal.”

“He was the only one who really saw the bubble for what it was.”

“If it wasn't for his contrarian thinking, we would have been swept away with the rest of the bubble companies.”

quoted_text:
Chamath says IP and software were "effectively rendered worthless" this week, after people decompiled Adobe's core products and published open-source versions, as every service goes headless

"The more important point I want to make though, is I sent this to Nick, there's been a couple things that happened in the last couple days, which I think are incredibly important."

"There have been people that decompiled the entire, the entire big five. What is the big five? Adobe has five very, very important products in their product suite. Freeberg may know them all, but I just know Photoshop. There's like a bunch of others. Okay."

"And these folks decompiled it, distilled it, and published open source versions of these things. And Rust, yeah. And I was so shocked, because I was like, hold on a second, these are like profound products that have existed and have had moats for years, and now they're just open source versions."

"And then Nikita was, I think, trolling, and he was building on that idea, and just talking about GTA, because it's about to get released. I think GTA 6 is about to come out, and we'll reconstruct this."

"Why is this important?"

"I think that IP and software was effectively rendered worthless two days ago."

"Because if you think about it, when everything is headless, so when Elon makes his services headless, Benioff made Salesforce headless a few months earlier, when all of these things are headless, and you can wrap them in agent tools, and you can connect them via MCP to other experiences, the value of IP does no longer exist in software. It doesn't exist."

"And I think that probably is the most profound implication."

"So, like, even in our business, we would argue with some of our customers all the time, because we'll say, oh, we'll build this for you, we'll own the IP. They'll say, no, we want the IP. We don't know how to negotiate it. And two days ago, I walked into the 8090 guys, I said, who cares? Who cares? But before, it was always a negotiation and a set of trade-offs. Now it's a who-cares thing, where, like, the IP is irrelevant."

"It still takes a while for the machinery of a business, and frankly the market, to understand. But that is the most important thing that happened this week in AI, in my opinion."

text:
Which of my personal agents was proactive in the right ways?

Most of my friends wouldn’t trust an AI agent with access to their personal email and calendar.

But in service of laziness (and science!), I gave a few agents read access to mine to see what they'd do without prompting.

✅ dot caught that I'd put a doctor's appointment on my calendar for the wrong day. It noticed that an appointment confirmation email I’d just received did not match what was in my calendar.
❌ That same day, Muse sent me a redundant notification about a stranger tagging me on someone else's GitHub gist. My GitHub handle is @.michelle, so I get mistakenly tagged by strangers all the time. Muse also surfaced the appointment confirmation email, but missed the date mismatch.
🟡 GrokBot hasn't notified me about anything to date. To be fair, I haven't asked it to, and silence is arguably better than what Muse is doing.

Useful proactivity > leaving me alone >>> noisy proactivity.

It was cool that dot looked across multiple sources to figure out what was worthy of a push notification.

author: tarunchitra
quoted_text:
I think of my goal as a mathematician as something like: to better understand the fundamental concepts “shape” and “number,” and to convey that understanding to others. I think this is a valuable goal for many reasons. The primary reason discussed on social media is the (admittedly slow, but I think very real) diffusion of mathematical ideas into technologies that better our lives. There are others, though: production of human capital (which plays some role in this diffusion), and diffusion of mathematical understanding into culture, for example. It is not obvious to me that even the bare technological need for mathematics can be filled without human experts; this seems to me to be a tricky question of institutional design.

For me the most compelling reason is simply that we feel a pressing need to understand. While deep understanding is largely limited to professional mathematicians, the existence of mathematicians and of the institutions they make up is a huge part of what makes mathematical understanding available to those who want it. I believe that the capacity to understand mathematics (and the universe as a whole) is part of a good life, and we should try to provide people with a good life. 

We operationalize the goal of understanding in a number of ways, problem-solving and theorem-proving among them. My own research is oriented around certain open questions that I believe measure our lack of understanding (of numbers, shapes and so on), and I think resolving those is genuinely important. I would welcome a solution with any provenance. But I think proof is only a measure of progress—what actually matters (for technology, human capital, culture, a good life) is a bit harder to get at. 

Crucially it is very hard to measure progress—plausibly theorem-proving is used in large part because it is easy to measure rather than because it is a perfect proxy for what we care about. I worry a bit that we may automate many easy-to-measure things without automating the correlates we care about for which they are proxies. This presents a clear problem for the design of institutions aimed at achieving progress.

In part because I think problem-solving is a proxy for something else, I don’t feel that my goal of understanding “shape” and “number” is particularly threatened by a machine that is good at problem solving. I expect that machine to be a substantial boon, instead. Ultimately I think we will operationalize mathematical progress in better ways. But how to do this is a difficult question  and I think many on here are too quick to dismiss concerns about it.

text:
还有一天伟大的 Hyperliquid 公平发射金融实验就要开始了：交易 1000x 永续合约用亏损挖矿。

和21 年老登们熟悉的合约挖矿盘 dydx 不一样的地方是：dydx v3 挖矿靠的是手续费和持仓，papertrade 只看亏损数量，早期锚定 1 USD亏损 对应 100 $PAPER

用白皮书的说法，整个协议的核心创新点是Martingaler，也就是用“延期兑付的债权＋代币激励”，让一个与用户对赌的资金池能够从零启动。

传统的资金盘，需要提前准备一笔本金。用户盈利时，平台要有钱立即支付，因此能接受的仓位和潜在赔付往往受到资金池规模限制。启动一个新平台，还要先解决“谁提供这笔钱、如何补偿提供者”的问题。

@papertrade_xyz  的方案是：允许交易继续发生，把暂时支付不起的盈利明确记成债务，按 FIFO 队列顺序等待偿付。

刚开始的阶段只能通过官方的 relayer 下单，不能直接和合约交互。但是看起来 relayer 的 api 已经悄悄上线，手快的可以准备起来了 👀

感谢 @0xanonnnn 老师喊我研究这个新盘子 😘

Token2049，被 CX最多的是一个矿币：Pearl @prlnet pearl-2:native 

它的逻辑很简单，比特币矿工烧电算哈希，算完就扔。Pearl说，既然要用电，不如算点有用的，让矿工算矩阵乘法，也就是大模型推理的底层运算，一边计算，一边挖矿。

声称完全公平启动，没有预挖、没有创始人分配、没有VC轮。

总体听下来，有多重叙事逻辑：

① "AI版比特币"：由算力和能源担保的数字货币，远期押注AI原生储值和算力结算。

② 能源迁移：比特币矿企正在把场地转租给AI数据中心，上半年减少了约75 EH/s算力。Pearl和AI同向，生态位更优。

③ "2-for-1"经济学：同一次GPU计算，既赚推理收入又挖PRL，推理价格更低→需求更多→算力更多→产出更多PRL。

但有一个根本问题：
Pearl的协议无法区分矿工算的是真实AI推理任务，还是随机生成的矩阵。
创始人自己也承认：“让矿工自选矩阵必然允许垃圾挖矿。”
目前流通约4.5亿枚PRL，占总供应16%，FDV 28亿美元，每天新增约135-140万美元代币供应，只上了几家小所，后续应该陆续会上大所。
