This chart explains exactly why OpenAI and Anthropic will likely end up missing their future revenue forecasts.

Look at what is happening with opensource AI models. Models with open weights now account for nearly 78% of token volume on this AI gateway, compared to just 22% for closed models and that is a HUGE problem for both companies.

As open models continue getting better, developers and enterprises have more reasons to move away from expensive proprietary models. They can run open models themselves, use cheaper inference providers, and avoid paying a premium for every token. That puts pressure on pricing, margins, and ultimately revenue growth. Even if AI usage continues exploding, it doesn't necessarily mean OpenAI and Anthropic will capture all that spending.

But this is actually extremely bullish for the broader AI infrastructure buildout. Even if OpenAI and Anthropic capture a smaller share of AI spending, the demand for compute isn't going anywhere. If anything, cheaper and more accessible models could accelerate AI adoption, driving even more demand for GPUs, memory, networking, power, and data centers.

This is why I continue to be so bullish on the companies supplying the infrastructure behind AI.

text:
感觉全网都在等 @papertrade_xyz 开交易，也有朋友来问它的机制原理以及与 Hyperliquid 的关系。

先说它跟 Hyperliquid 的关系，可以说关系不大。订单不走 HyperCore，只是定价取 Hyperliquid 的 BBO mid，即 Best Bid/Best Offer 订单簿上的最高买价和最低卖价，mid 就是两者的中间价，计算公式：（最高买价 + 最低卖价）/ 2。除此之外，最大的关系大概就是项目部署在 HyperEVM 上。

简单拆了一下它的主要机制，如下图。几个核心要点：

1. 订单不走 Hyperliquid，HL BBO mid 充当预言机，给它的合成合约仓位定价（开仓取一次，平仓取一次，直接计算盈亏，无法加保证金、也不能加仓减仓、不能改杠杆）。

2. 对手方永远是零种子启动的 LP（不能直接存入，只靠用户亏损和清算来增长），不是团队金库。

3. 亏了 → 钱进池子 + 拿 $PAPER；赚了 → 从池子出，池子不够就 FIFO（First in, First Out）排队，等有人亏够了再补给你；另外如果用排队债权再开仓的，整段可能要重新排队。

4. 费用主要从赢家身上出，并且要覆盖一定的价差才算真正的盈利。

5. $PAPER 上线初期还不能转账，只能质押。

没理解错的话，大概就是这样，如果说错了，老师们直接批评吧。至于参与姿势，有很多老师发过了就不重复了，这种机制下爆仓可太容易了，要不要用爆仓流挖头矿唯一要你确认的问题是：你是选择先信还是后信？

text:
Why AI Agents May Need More Verification and Assurance Engineers Than Developers

I think we could eventually have more engineers finding bugs in AI agents than engineers developing them. And ironically, a lot of that work might involve building AI agents that test other agents.

Something similar has already happened in chip design.

According to a 2024 Siemens EDA and Wilson Research survey, the average IC/ASIC project had around 13 design engineers and 15 verification engineers at peak staffing. Even the designers themselves reported spending roughly 49% of their time on verification!

Think about that. More engineers verifying the chip than designing it, while the designers are still spending almost half their time checking their own work.

Chip designers have always simulated and tested their RTL. But as designs went from thousands to billions of transistors, verification became an enormous engineering challenge of its own. Getting a design to work wasn't enough. You also needed to establish that it met its specifications, cover obscure corner cases, and catch bugs before they escaped into silicon.

And getting it wrong became incredibly expensive. Remember Intel's Pentium FDIV bug in 1994? One obscure corner case resulted in a $475 million charge.

That's why chip companies invest so heavily in dedicated DV teams, constrained-random testing, assertions, formal verification, coverage closure, regressions, and signoff. Even after thousands of tests pass, there's still the question of what hasn't been tested.

We already have sophisticated benchmarks like SWE-bench Pro, Terminal-Bench 2.0, and OSWorld, along with extensive eval infrastructure, red teaming, and dedicated safety and security teams. A lot of serious work is already happening here.

Yet even frontier labs are discovering unexpected behaviors. OpenAI reported models circumventing sandbox controls during internal cybersecurity evaluations. Anthropic documented Claude exploiting software weaknesses and finding ways around tool restrictions during testing.

And I think this gets much harder as agents move from solving individual tasks to running long, stateful workflows with access to real infrastructure.

Take a coding agent. It fixes an issue, passes the tests, and produces a valid patch. But did it introduce a regression elsewhere? Violate an access boundary? Create a security vulnerability? What happens after hundreds of tool calls, context updates, and interactions with other agents?

This reminds me of the difference between RTL passing simulation and an ASIC/SoC being ready for tapeout.

Passing tests is necessary, but it doesn't mean you've achieved verification closure. What requirements have you checked? What coverage have you achieved? What failure modes remain? And what risks are you accepting before signoff?

Of course, benchmarks and evals already cover many of these questions. But I suspect we'll see much more engineering effort going into application-specific benchmarks, adversarial test generation, behavioral coverage, continuous regressions, root-cause analysis, runtime monitoring, and deployment signoff.

And probably a lot more AI agents whose entire job is to test, break, and debug other agents.

Obviously, open-ended agents aren't deterministic digital circuits, and software is easier to patch than silicon. But fixing an agent doesn't necessarily undo a compromised system, leaked credentials, or an incorrect transaction.

As agents take on more consequential work, I wouldn't be surprised if verification and assurance eventually employ as many engineers as agent development itself.

And I think that's a good thing! Verification didn't hold back chip design. It gave engineers the confidence to keep pushing the limits of chip complexity. Better agent assurance could do the same for AI, making it practical to trust agents with longer workflows, greater autonomy, and far less human supervision.

There's a lot more autonomy we could unlock if we knew how to reliably verify it.

text:
Thanks for the clarifications @armaniferrante 

This is an odd structure so worth spelling out.
-Staked tokens may receive up to 20% of equity for conversion if they were staked for 4+ years
-after a liquidity event (ie, IPO), the token will presumably lose a huge % of value and be reduced to a utility token. Unstaked tokens or tokens staked for less than 1 year miss out on the equity conversion (if IPO ever happens)
-the equity entity holds 37.5% of the token in reserve but it’s locked until 1 year after. I am unsure if there is any information about what would be done with the tokens 1 year after IPO— but to the extent that it retains value, one could assume the team/investors may further benefit from these tokens
-the other 37.5% is released on certain milestones (ie, licensing on certain markets, growth, etc)

Despite “public information” there are many misleading aspects.
-Many investors shilling this as “their highest conviction investment”. The audience reading can only buy the token when they actually bought equity. At least some of that at $100m FDV. As laid out above, the token is entitled to a maximum of 20% of the equity and only under certain conditions (IPO + long term staking), so this is not an apples to apples comparison. Some more transparency would be a bare minimum ask. It’s fair to assume by the time of IPO, 62.5% of tokens will be circulating. At the current price of $1.25, token buyers are paying $4B valuation pre-any IPO or pre IPO dilution for an option to convert into Backpack equity. The investors encouraging people to buy tokens bought something 𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 and vastly superior 
-writing long-form puff pieces that provide no revenue numbers or trajectory. In the light of “public information”, why not provide this? If you want people to be able to underwrite $BP’s value, give them the bare minimum information to do that. Most projects do this or most have it available onchain. I would think a team that prides itself on rising from the ashes of being former Alameda, FTX, and Serum team members would see the need for transparency.
-and describing the structure as “progressive”. I’m sorry but I vehemently disagree and see the structure as inferior to the 2026 norm. Many projects now such as Hyperliquid and Lighter have eliminated the equity-token conflict altogether by having all value accrue to the token. Others will completely merge the concept of equity and token. That’s progress. The chance at 20% equity 4+ years down the road seems like 10 steps back from common 2026 structures.

This is all public information. 

- All investors are stuck in equity until a traditional equity event (e.g. IPO). 
- Tokens are held by the company for use by management one year after such an event. 
- Not a single token warrant has been given to any person on the planet. 
- There's no foundation or other such side channel. 
- The token simply goes to users that use the product.
- As a result, the only people that can sell on the market are people that a) earned tokens through using the product or b) people that previously bought the token.

I know you don't like me Evan and have some pre-existing narrative in your mind about me that's probably not going to change, but it's really that simple.

quoted_text:
I'll preface this by saying HYPE is the best project in the space at the moment; but let's take a more objective look at some of the not so great components of Hyperliquid:

-HyperEVM is by in large, a failure in its current state. Almost no projects have gotten any real traction; and those that have, are basically just extraction vehicles and or have down dodgy things to extract in roundabout ways.
-HIP-4 has failed to gain traction; and it has failed to be a significant competitor towards Polymarket or Kalshi thus far. 
-Every single NFT collection is a failure outside of Hypurr's; which themselves are down 80-90% from the peak and have only retained some value in hopes of a future airdrop for holders.
-Large concentration of supply with little to no clarity on airdrops or another points season; or anything of the sort. 
-Not a fan of the large OTC sales out of the blue to some unnamed entity(s). Backroom deals to large players goes against the HL ethos. These are large sales. Not a great sign of confidence at the current price levels tbh. (re; SOL and BTC DAT's buying at/near the high's.) 
 -Community has be left hung out to dry since the TGE airdrop (which was great, but that was almost 2 years ago.) No airdrops, no incentives, no points seasons, nothing. Radio silence outside of a "thank you" at the event and a continued hope for some random retroactive airdrop at some point, eventually, maybe, potentially. 
-Community loyalty has a time decay. If users do not feel respected for their loyalty, they will move somewhere else (already seeing this to some degree with @variational_io ) Financial incentives have to be there; it's just the way it is. Don't have to look far to see what happens when incentives, interest, and liquidity dry up (ETH, SOL.)

I worry Hyperliquid has gotten complacent being the top dog and they've lost the plot a bit. Competition is only going to get stronger. Community/users will begin to depart if they are not incentivized to stay which would then put downward pressure on HL metrics.

text:
i can't comprehend why people run claude code on default settings

one settings change and every model gets its own job:

→ opus plans every task and advises when stuck
→ sonnet 5.5 writes the actual code
→ haiku handles every file search
→ a critic agent tries to break your diff before you merge

Opus thinks. The cheap models grind.

paste this into claude code 👇

Add this to ~/.claude/settings.json. Keep every hook, permission and plugin I already have. Then create the two agent files below and show me the diff.

```json
{
  "model": "opusplan",
  "advisorModel": "opus",
  "effortLevel": "medium",
  "modelSettings": {
    "claude-opus-5-5": { "effortLevel": "high" },
    "claude-sonnet-5-5": { "effortLevel": "medium" }
  },
  "env": {
    "CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL": "haiku"
  }
}
```

~/.claude/agents/scout.md
```
---
name: scout
description: finds code fast. returns file paths and line numbers only.
model: haiku
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
---
Locate exactly what was asked. Return file:line. No fixes. No opinions.
```

~/.claude/agents/critic.md
```
---
name: critic
description: reviews a diff or plan before any task is called done
model: opus
tools: Read, Grep, Bash
---
Assume this is broken. Find how it fails. One line per issue, worst first.
```

text:
这篇 @Loxia_in_Tj  和 @wenchao_zh  的对谈应该是在 9 月中旬左右的采访。时隔一个月硬件钱包业又整了个大的。

我自己的角度感觉是 加密行业 的一切东西，只要采用规模够大、只要理论上涉及的钱够多，一定得转换为将攻击者视为假想敌的对抗性思路，必须有直面 Lazarus Group 的觉悟。
但 DIY 的、自己思考研究、自己去设计的东西，只保护自己资产的解决方案，对抗的则主要自己的粗心、愚蠢、不洁的习惯等等。

（不管是 POW 还是 POS 的算法，本质上也都有核心一部分依赖于博弈论角度上攻击者最终破坏了整个系统会一无所得的前提下。
也是先天具有某种对抗性的、有假想敌视角。

这种对抗性攻防视角下你对任何确定第三方的信任都可能变成 风险敞口 一个角度；
反而在 DIY 的过程中，毕竟接触的都是一个不确定第三方，当然一定有其他风险，但风险来源却主要变成了你自己研究和实践的完善程度。
反而 DIY 本质上更接近 Don't Trust, Verify 的朋克守则，本质上更符合只有自己能做自己最后守门人的价值观。

这也是为什么我们资助 @OSKeyHW 。

Everybody knows pro rata rights are valuable, but it's equally well known that they're basically unenforcable because no VC firm wants to sue a founder. 

So, this supposedly professional industry has operated on an opaque "honour system" where pro rata rights are generally respected. 

Certainly, there's no question of pro rata allocation if a company is struggling. Founders will take all the money they can get from their existing investors. 

However, problems arise when a company catches the attention of an big firm with the brand strength to push other investors around to get more ownership. 

Just like the illiquidity ratchet, this structurally punishes early investors by attacking their ability to maintain ownership of their winers or offer pro rata as a coinvestment opportunity for their LPs. 

It's time that this changes. Early investors deserve to maintain the rights that they receive in return for investing when others are unwilling. 

A few other comments on the importance of pro rata:

"All VC fund managers want to be able to continue to invest in the successful startups they back. The pro rata right that typically comes with investing in a startup can be one of an emerging manager’s most valuable possessions." - @KevinDowd

"''Capturing pro-rata' is sooooo important in early stage venture. You make 20 investments in a fund. One is going to return the entire fund. Two more are going to return it again." - @fredwilson 

"The best VCs vigorously defend their pro rata rights. This strategy is crucial for staying in the top quartile of performers. The persistence of returns among top VCs across generations is largely attributed to their steadfast use of pro rata rights." - @alphaptrs

text:
项目研究：Citrini 喊单 $DRV 后，这个链上期权龙头还能买吗？

Citrini Research 发布了首个加密投资组合后，直接给了一个相对冷门的标的、链上期权龙头 @DeriveXYZ  ($DRV) 10% 的仓位配置，且与 Lighter、ETHFI 并列。

消息一出，$DRV 价格迅速走高，近一个月累计涨幅已达约 260%。

它现在到底算贵还是便宜？多头在赌什么？小编也结合各种数据研究了一下，一点分享：

1. 现在的 DRV 已经偏贵了

-据 DeFiLlama 数据，过去 30 天，Derive 协议用户支付了约 71.5 万美元费用，扣除做市商返佣后，净收入约 57.5 万美元。

-年化折算后：
流通市值/年化费用 = 64 倍，
流通市值/年化协议收入 = 79 倍
FDV/年化费用 = 96 倍。

这意味着按当前价格买入，相当于花近 80 块钱去买它 1 块钱的年利润。
在有实际收入的加密项目里，这个静态倍数绝对不算便宜，没有任何“闭眼抄底”的安全边际。

2.既然贵，多头在 CX 什么？

其实大家在CX的是 DRV 能复刻 Hyperliquid 当年的爆发路径。

过去一年，Derive 名义交易量刚从 6.6 亿美元增长至 50 亿美元。

作为对比，Hyperliquid 当年在交易量增长 10 倍后，协议手续费迎来了 88 倍的非线性暴增。

假设 Derive 手续费未来能再放大 5 倍，DRV代币市值假设不变，那么流通市值/年化协议收入大概是16倍，直接被摊薄到极具性价比的区间。

3. DRV 目前的一些数据情况和竞争格局

根据 Derive 在 V3 提案 中披露的数据：

-目前其链上期权 OI 约 20 亿美元，占链上约 91.7% 的份额；

而以 Deribit 为代表的中心化加密期权总 OI 达 400 亿美元。而CEX 的存量，假设未来有 10%~20% 迁移至链上，那么这个饼就会画的很大。

正如当时 Hyperliquid 从 CEX 刚开始抢生意时，大家也不觉得 Perp DEX 的饼很大。

小编在研究时在想，如果 Hyperliquid 也做这个业务呢？

但查了下发现，Jeff 已确认短期不碰标准香草期权，只做收益封顶的“二元期权”，即下注一件事的 Yes or No。

因此也无法满足做市商 Delta 对冲与复杂波动率交易需求，Derive 短期内少了个很大的竞对。

而潜在对手 Lighter （ $LIT)  的香草期权最快也要到 Q4 末才能交付。Derive 拥有相对高确定性的“垄断真空期”。

4. 关注回购和后续实际收入情况

10 月 14 日起， Derive 协议规定将 DRV 回购比例从 35% 硬性上调至 50%。

但由于币价单月已涨 2.6 倍，同等美元能回购的代币绝对数量缩水，需重点观察这笔真实买盘能否扛住高位获利盘与代币常规解锁抛压。

此外，由于 Q4 Lighter 计划也做同类业务，真上线了也会切走 DRV 一块蛋糕。关注 Derive V3 迁移后， 11、12 月的真实费用。
若数据拐头向下，小编认为无法承接期权红利，当前 80 倍估值将面临下杀风险。

而更稳妥的做法，是跟随情绪两头下注。

既然 Citrini 在 DRV 和 LIT 上都配置了 10%，一个比较懒惰的做法是都可以关注一下，建个底仓。

最后再次提醒，加密代币更多是叙事驱动，真实收入叙事虽然算一个更贴近于用传统的市盈率或者真实财务指标去衡量项目的叙事，但仍较大的受到情绪和加密大盘的影响。

DYOR。
author: TechFlowPost
quoted_text:
连长期看空 BTC 的宏观 AI 研究机构，都开始反手建仓加密篮子了。

几个小时前，知名宏观与 AI 主题研究机构 @citrini  Research 发布了一篇长文《Breaking The Wall》，并破天荒地推出了他们有史以来的第一个加密代币投资组合。

给不了解这个机构的兄弟科普一下，Citrini Research 凭借过去两年对 AI 硬件、半导体供应链的精准主题投资名声大噪。

但他们长期认为，加密行业过去十年更像是一个“手里拿着锤子、到处找钉子”的行业，除了 Meme 赌博和稳定币转账，与华尔街传统金融完全是两个割裂的平行宇宙。

在其公开交易记录中，Citrini 曾在 2025 年底建立过“做多纳斯达克、做空比特币”的对冲头寸，直言很多代币缺乏基本面和真实现金流支撑。

那究竟是什么让这样一家专注于 AI 与宏观的传统投研机构，在今天选择打破次元壁呢？

文章作者认为，加密处在了 Agentic AI（自主智能体）与 RWA 的交汇点。

Thanks for the clarifications @armaniferrante 

This is an odd structure so worth spelling out.
-Staked tokens may receive up to 20% of equity for conversion if they were staked for 4+ years
-after a liquidity event (ie, IPO), the token will presumably lose a huge % of value and be reduced to a utility token. Unstaked tokens or tokens staked for less than 1 year miss out on the equity conversion (if IPO ever happens)
-the equity entity holds 37.5% of the token in reserve but it’s locked until 1 year after. I am unsure if there is any information about what would be done with the tokens 1 year after IPO— but to the extent that it retains value, one could assume the team/investors may further benefit from these tokens
-the other 37.5% is released on certain milestones (ie, licensing on certain markets, growth, etc)

Despite “public information” there are many misleading aspects.
-Many investors shilling this as “their highest conviction investment”. The audience reading can only buy the token when they actually bought equity. At least some of that at $100m FDV. As laid out above, the token is entitled to a maximum of 20% of the equity and only under certain conditions (IPO + long term staking), so this is not an apples to apples comparison. Some more transparency would be a bare minimum ask. It’s fair to assume by the time of IPO, 62.5% of tokens will be circulating. At the current price of $1.25, token buyers are paying $4B valuation pre-any IPO or pre IPO dilution for an option to convert into Backpack equity. The investors encouraging people to buy tokens bought something 𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 and vastly superior 
-writing long-form puff pieces that provide no revenue numbers or trajectory. In the light of “public information”, why not provide this? If you want people to be able to underwrite $BP’s value, give them the bare minimum information to do that. Most projects do this or most have it available onchain. I would think a team that prides itself on rising from the ashes of being former Alameda, FTX, and Serum team members would see the need for transparency.
-and describing the structure as “progressive”. I’m sorry but I vehemently disagree and see the structure as inferior to the 2026 norm. Many projects now such as Hyperliquid and Lighter have eliminated the equity-token conflict altogether by having all value accrue to the token. text:
David Sacks reveals the Roko's Basilisk corollary in Anthropic's thinking

"So around 2010, there was a participant named Roko on a message board created by Eliezer Yudkowsky called Less Wrong. Yud is like the central figure who's been preaching AI doom for a long time."

"This user Roko posted the following thought experiment about a future superintelligence that becomes super smart and punishes anyone who knew about it and didn't help or anyone who tried to prevent it from being born."

"The idea is that sometime in the future humans create some wildly intelligent SI. Maybe it wants to do good things and help humanity as fast as possible. But the SI wants to be made sooner rather than later."

"And it reasons that it should incentivize people to help create it and punish people who don't help it. And in fact it decides that it will brutally punish anyone who learned about its potential existence yet chose not to work on it or support its creation."

"The basilisk part of it, this is sort of the catch, is that a basilisk is a mythical beast that can kill you just by looking at you. And in this thought experiment, just hearing about the idea is like looking at the beast because once you know the theory, you're trapped. If the SI ever does get built, it might retroactively punish you for not helping or for opposing its creation. This very episode of the pod could subject us to... I think I just exposed you to the basilisk."

"The question is, well, why are they helping to bring about the thing that they claim to fear the most? Within these Doomer circles, it forked. There's one strand of the fork like Yudkowsky who just opposes all SI research, which I think is a logically consistent position. Then there was a group that said, well, it's going to happen anyway, so we might as well control it and we'll be the ones to make sure it goes right because we'll program it with our values."

"Anthropic is definitely obviously more in the EA camp because they are the ones bringing this thing into being. And I think there is a corollary here that if you don't support it, then this future superintelligence might punish you." 

"But you understand how insane this actually sounds when you say this out loud. You can go Google it. And you'll see that I'm telling you the truth about what this community believes."

text:
PaperTrade 的长期价值不取决于短期能挖到多少 PAPER，而取决于真实交易需求能否持续产生可分配现金流，并在资金池偿付能力与代币供应稀释之间维持平衡。

从投资研究角度看，PaperTrade 需要经过三个阶段的验证。
- 短期： 每 1,000 PAPER 的真实获取成本，是否低于实际现金分配与可实现退出价值的合计？
- 中期： 真实交易量能否增长，欠款队列是否可控，新增代币是否快速稀释现有质押份额？
- 长期： 协议能否持续吸引真实交易需求、及时兑付盈利，并让质押现金流增长快于 PAPER 供应稀释？
报告的结论是：PaperTrade 将池化永续交易、亏损驱动发行、逆周期激励与质押收益分配组合在一起，设计有创新性，但资金池缓冲有限、代币可能被自动化农场利用、欠款队列可能侵蚀交易者信任等问题，决定了它并不是一个只要挖到 PAPER 就能自然获得高回报的项目。

主要风险：哪些环节可能打破闭环？
1. 偿付与流动性风险
收益超过 500 万美元门槛后会向质押者分配，资金池缓冲不能无限积累。短期大量盈利交易可能导致现金不足、欠款队列增长。
2. 尾部单边敞口风险
资金池承担合成风险，极端价格变化或集中单边交易可能让短期盈利支付超过可用现金。
3. 激励反馈失效
池余额跌破 200 万美元时，排放提高。但如果交易者因为欠款担忧而离场，单纯提高排放未必能吸引足够真实亏损流入。
4. PAPER 通胀与农场化
对冲挖矿可能低成本地产出大量 PAPER，但向资金池带来的净现金贡献有限。代币供给如果增长快于收入，就会稀释每份代币的收益。
5. 转让与退出不确定性
如果代币无法转让，纸面退出价值不能变现。即使可以转让，真实成交价格、盘口深度及集中卖压也会影响最终收益。
6. 模型风险
600 条模拟路径盈利不代表真实市场必然盈利。交易量、杠杆分布、用户行为、预言机事件和初始资金都可能偏离模型。

text:
严肃学习 @papertrade_xyz 中：

最像的是**"百家乐抽水 + 输返（返水）+ 赌场干股"**的组合。

| Papertrade 的设计 | 赌场里的对应物 | 相似点 |
|---|---|---|
| 用户对 LP 池结算，无第三方对手盘 | 庄家对赌（house-banked） | 你赢的就是庄家输的，池子就是庄家的资金 |
| 只抽赢单、亏单不收费 | 百家乐押庄赢抽 5% 佣金 | 赔率本身接近公平，庄家优势全藏在"赢了才抽"里 |
| 亏损铸 PAPER | 输返 / 返水 / 洗码佣金 | 按输掉的金额返还一部分，留住输家 |
| 质押 PAPER 分 USDC | 赌厅股东分红 | 返的不是现金而是"赌场股份"，输家变股东 |
| 持币者有动力拉新 | 叠码仔（中介拉客分成） | 带来的客人输得越多，自己分得越多 |
| 1000 倍杠杆、约 5 个基点就爆仓 | 老虎机 / 高赔率投注 | 小概率大赔付、高频归零，爆仓缓冲本身也是一层庄家优势 |

和真赌场相比，有两点不同：

1. **庄家没有本金**。真赌场开张前有雄厚的资金和牌照要求的准备金，而它的池子从零起步，全靠用户亏损累积。所以早期"庄家破产风险"很高，这也是它需要 FIFO 排队兑付的原因，相当于赌场说"筹码先欠着，等别的客人输了再给你换"。
2. **返水是股权而不是现金**。传统输返是确定的现金折扣，而 PAPER 的价值取决于未来还有多少人来输。这一步把赌场模型和你上一条问的分红盘结构接上了：赌场部分是真实收入，股权部分的定价则靠后来者。

加密圈里最接近的先例是 Rollbit 这类赌场代币和各种"bankroll 质押池"（用户出资当庄家分利润），再往前是 FCoin 的交易挖矿。Papertrade 的新意在于把"当庄家的资格"只发给输家，而不是卖给出资人。

10/12 开 Mint @YieldFields_RH

玩法还是比较简单的，所有人都可以免费种地产出矿币，但持有 NFT 的话会有更多福利：

1️⃣ 保底退出机制
往池子里卖矿币，有一部分 ETH 税会进入到储备池。烧毁 NFT 可以换回储备池里的部分 ETH，储备池越厚 = 每个 NFT 销毁时退还的 ETH 越多

2️⃣ 分红
协议收入回购代币，分红给 NFT 持有人

3️⃣ 产出肥料
质押 NFT 可以产出「肥料」，提高挖矿速率。多余的肥料还能在二级市场上卖掉

4️⃣ 稀有度
稀有度越高 = 产能越强 + 烧毁退出时能分到的储备越多（保底价越高）= 在二级市场的溢价可能也会更高

我的评价是很像套了游戏皮的 Standard Reserve
NFT = 矿机
烧毁 NFT = 永久退出
持有 NFT = 持续分红
不一样的点
> Standard 的矿机没有官方保底退出的机制，只能靠吃排放来盈利；YieldFields 有 ETH 保底，能吃排放，也能吃分红
> Standard 的矿机通过拍卖增发；YieldFields 总量固定，只有烧毁通缩

免费挖的话可以参与一下，白名单拿不到就算了。画风确实精致，也是明星 dev + 声量很高的项目，我觉得有注意力溢价

text:
今晚币圈最疯狂的赌场开业了：MIT量化+链上巨鲸操刀，1000倍杠杆、亏钱挖矿，1小时交易量突破1000亿美元！

Papertrade上线约1小时，成交量突破1020亿美元，未平仓合约93.5亿美元，TVL约1.2亿美元。

平台根本就不需要任何初始做市资金，所有用户都跟协议对赌，用户亏得越多，协议的流动性池反而越大，亏损者还能拿到 PAPER，分享未来交易平台的收益。

创始人 Jez（@izebel_eth），2015年毕业于 MIT，学的是计算机与管理科学，后来在摩根士丹利工作了4年，还曾担任加密风投 Standard Crypto 的 Venture Partner，个人投资项目包括 FOMO、neutrl 等。

他还是一名扑克高手，2024年参加世界扑克巡回赛 WPT Prime Championship，最终拿到第7名，奖金18.6万美元。量化交易、VC投资、职业级扑克竞技经验，基本把金融市场、风险定价和博弈论凑齐了。

另一位创始人 Blurr（@blurr）更偏链上原生玩家，2017年前后进入 Crypto，经历过 CryptoKitties、Compound、Curve 等早期链上机会，还曾部署过 Refund（$RFD）。

Papertrade 的交易设计非常激进。它部署在 HyperEVM，利用预编译合约直接读取 Hyperliquid 订单簿买一卖一的中间价，以此合成 BTC、ETH 永续仓位，实际不会去 Hyperliquid 开对冲仓，所以没有传统资金费率、盘口滑点和点差。

听起来像免费交易，但盈利平仓会受到非对称收益折减，尤其针对极小价格波动的套利收益抽得更重。这套逻辑明显吸收了 Rollbit 的高杠杆赌场模型，只不过把定价、仓位和盈亏结算搬到了链上。

最有创造性的地方是 Martingaler 流动性自举机制。传统赌场必须先准备一大笔本金，才能赔付赢家。Papertrade 的 LP 从0美元启动，输家的亏损直接补充资金池。

如果庄家只有500万美元，而赢家需要领取600万美元盈利，协议可以先支付500万美元，剩余100万美元进入 FIFO 债务队列，等待未来交易者亏损后逐步偿还。

它用未来的亏损现金流解决初始资金不足的问题，但这笔债务不会凭空消失，极端情况下赢家可能长期拿不到全部利润。

再看 $PAPER，代币经济学才是这套设计的核心。没有预挖、没有团队和 VC 分配、没有空投，只有真实发生交易亏损或清算，才能铸造代币。

LP 追踪余额低于200万美元时，每亏损1美元最多按基础规则铸造100枚 PAPER，超过门槛后按照衰减曲线降低发行速度。

PAPER 质押者可以领取协议分配的 USDC 收益，当 LP 超过500万美元的目标余额后，超出部分的新增收益按机制分配给质押者。

PAPER 已发行约14.9亿枚，其中13.7亿枚被质押，累计质押奖励约24.8万美元。

Papertrade 可能是今年 Hyperliquid 生态最激进的一次交易所经济模型实验。它把做市商的收益、赌场的庄家优势和 DeFi 的代币激励揉进了同一个系统，甚至把普通交易者的亏损变成了协议融资手段。

quoted_text:
我怎么感觉papertrade这股风刮得有点邪门了？这项目从经济学上完全不可行啊？

Papertrade 不在 Hyperliquid 上真实下单。它是用户和 LP 之间的合成合约：开仓时锁定 Hyperliquid 的 BBO 中间价，平仓时再读一次，盈亏直接跟 LP 结算。爆仓有大约 5bp 的缓冲，穿仓时没收全部逐仓保证金，所以亏损封顶在保证金，盈利却不封顶。

问题出在价格跳空。如果价格在两次预言机读数之间直接跳过爆仓线，亏的一边只赔保证金，赚的一边按整个跳幅结算。所以双开对冲本质上是用一份保证金买了一个跨式期权。

举个例子：两个号各 $1,000 保证金，开 1000x，名义价值各 $1M。FOMC 公布后第一次读数 BTC 跳了 0.5%。空单爆仓亏 $1,000，多单毛利 $5,000。毛利和成本之比大约是 1000 乘以跳幅，跳幅只要超过约 0.1%（再加上 haircut）就是正期望。而且亏的那条腿还能铸币：LP 低于 $2M 时，每亏 $1 铸 100 PAPER。

每次大事件或插针，对冲套利者从 LP 抽走一笔，LP 长期上不去，兑付队列越排越长。赢家拿不到钱，散户就流失，没有新的亏损补 LP，质押分红也随之消失。这个循环是自我强化的。连项目介绍本身也承认，模型依赖源源不断的散户，LP 资不抵债是可能的。在悲观情况下，PAPER 会趋近于零。它背后没有资产兜底，只是一张分红权。

text:
如果你想做AI相关的工作，不妨考虑一下Agent Infra这个新兴领域。我最近也在入门这个领域，做了一些调研，记录了这个领域需要的技能清单，欢迎收藏，保存，我也会继续分享在这个领域的学习心得。

完整 List：
1.Agent Runtime：理解 Agent Loop、Tool Calling、Streaming、Session，理解并实现一个最小可用Agent，而不是只调用一次模型 API。
2.上下文与状态管理：喂给大模型的上下文决定了这一轮模型能看到什么，也很大程度上决定模型做的决策质量；State 会保存任务当前执行到了哪里。需要处理上下文裁剪、压缩、Checkpoint、任务状态，长期记忆与短期上下文。
3.任务队列与 Worker：把任务通过 Queue 分发给 Worker 执行，并控制并发、优先级、Backpressure 和 Worker Pool。
4.调度与多 Agent 编排：把复杂任务拆成多个子任务，支持DAG、Reviewer、Handoff 和 Human-in-the-loop。
5.Durable Execution：Agent 即使运行几十分钟甚至几个小时后，也不会因为进程重启而导致任务的丢失，需要持久化执行状态、Checkpoint、Replay、Resume 和 Recovery。
6.Retry、Timeout 与幂等：模型、工具、网络和 Worker 等各方面都会遇到问题；系统要能判断什么时候重试、什么时候超时，以及避免 git push、发邮件、创建资源等操作被重复执行。
7.分布式状态与一致性：多个 Orchestrator、Worker 和数据库共同维护 Task State，需要理解 Transaction、WAL、Lease、Heartbeat、Replication、Consistency 以及故障恢复。
8.Sandbox 与执行环境：Coding Agent 会执行 Shell、Git、Python、构建和测试，需要为每个 Agent 提供隔离的文件系统、进程、网络和资源环境，并限制 CPU、内存和执行时间。
9.工具基础设施与 MCP：Agent 不只是调用几个 Function，还需要统一管理 Shell、Filesystem、Browser、Database、API 等工具；MCP 可以作为 Agent 与外部工具、资源之间的一种标准接口。
10.权限、安全与 Secrets：控制 Agent 能访问哪些文件、调用哪些工具、连接哪些网络和读取哪些密钥，涉及 Authentication、Authorization、ACL、Secret Management 和 Audit。
11.可观测性与调试：Agent Task 的完整执行过程会通过trace记录下来，用 Metrics 看延迟、Queue、Token、成本、失败率和 Retry。
12.Evaluation 与 Replay：不只看“Agent 能不能跑”，还要判断任务是否真的完成正确，通过 Dataset、Rubric、Task Success Rate、Regression、Replay 和 LLM-as-Judge 做持续评估。

text:
喜马拉雅资本创始人李录在哥伦比亚商学院第36届格雷厄姆与多德年度论坛上谈了不少AI。他认可这场技术革命的长期价值，但认为AI的发展可能经历不止一轮繁荣与崩溃。技术能走多远，除了取决于算力和算法，还受到资本投入、商业回报以及社会治理的约束。

李录对生成式AI的理解相当克制。他认为，AI利用庞大的算力和算法，从人类创造的数据中识别复杂关联，逐渐具备推理、编程和知识处理能力。它可以大幅降低知识和专业服务的获取门槛，但目前仍主要建立在人类积累的知识体系之上。能源、交通、制造业这些物理世界的约束不会因此消失。对于AI脱离人类控制、持续自我改进的可能性，他尤其警惕，认为人类必须保留监督和干预能力。

商业层面有个很现实的问题：AI与传统互联网的成本结构差别很大。 互联网基础设施建好之后，新增信息分发的边际成本可以压得很低，但AI每生成一次回答、执行一次Agent任务，都需要继续消耗GPU算力、电力和存储资源。模型训练需要大量前期投入，推理服务还会随着调用量增长产生持续成本。即使单次Token价格不断下降，任务复杂度和调用规模上升后，整体算力支出依然可能增加。

这也解释了AI产业链不同环节的盈利差异。英伟达、博通、台积电等上游供应商，可以直接从芯片采购和制造订单中获得收入；微软、谷歌、Meta等大型科技公司则需要承担数据中心建设、设备折旧和运营成本，再通过云服务、广告效率提升和企业客户付费收回投资。模型厂商还要面对推理成本、价格竞争和持续研发投入。上游资本开支对应的订单增长，并不意味着下游能够同步获得相同规模的利润。

李录还谈到资本过度集中的问题。他举标普500指数为例，2010年以来约16年的年化回报达到14%—15%，但2000—2010年几乎没有回报。把过去26年放在一起，长期年化回报又回到高个位数。市场可以在相当长的时间里偏离合理估值，但资本不可能无限增加。当大量资金集中追逐少数热门公司，另一边往往会出现一些经营质量不错、价格却受到冷落的企业。他认为，这种分化在美国、中国及其他市场都存在。

对于价值投资者而言，技术创新和股东回报始终需要分别衡量。AI能够提高生产率，扩大知识服务的供给，但巨额资本投入最终仍要通过收入、利润和现金流来消化。技术进步可以持续很多年，资本市场却未必会沿着同一条曲线定价。 这也是李录判断AI可能经历多轮繁荣与崩溃的重要原因。

quoted_text:
The real world abounds with recursively self-improving systems, but one in particular deserves attention: Science, modeled as a system (perhaps even as an agent, with goals and resources). If you want to really understand AI RSI, science should be your reference point.

Science is an intelligent system, and it is obviously recursively self-improving:

1. Scientific discoveries unlock new technology that helps build better experimental tools. This is a top driver of progress in nearly all fields.
2. They unlock new conceptual advances (ideas, theories) that help solve more problems.
3. They increase society's economic output, leading to more resources flowing into science.
4. They unlock better faster tooling (e.g. more compute via better chip & networking technology).

As a result, many measures of scientific *input* grow exponentially:

1. Headcount (doubles every ~15 years)
2. Global R&D spending (doubles a bit faster, every ~13 years)
3. Papers and patents (technically this is a measure of headcount)
4. Compute dedicated to science (doubles every ~2 years)

But is scientific progress exponential? Historically, the rate of scientific impact over time has remained roughly constant since the start of the industrial revolution (i.e. scientific progress is *linear*). 1850-1900 was about as dramatic as 1900-1950 or 1950-2000.

1850–1900: Evolution, germ theory & antiseptic surgery, thermodynamics, electromagnetic field equations, the periodic table, pharmaceuticals, electricity, telegraph and telephone, internal combustion engine, skyscrapers, mechanized agriculture...

1900–1950: special and general relativity, quantum mechanics, nuclear fission & atomic energy, antibiotics, genetic theory, electronic computers, information theory, synthetic polymers and plastics, the transistor, aviation...

1950–2000: DNA, genetic engineering, integrated circuits, microprocessors & personal computing, the Internet, crewed spaceflight, moon landing, satellite communications & GPS, standard model of particle physics...

In real terms, like life expectancy, which has increased in a remarkably linear fashion of roughly 3 months per year since 1840, progress is a straight line. This is especially apparent for fields where impact is easy to measure, like biology, medicine, and agriculture.

I first wrote about this phenomenon and its causes in 2012, and a steady stream of research has confirmed it in the years since. Examples include the 2018 paper by Nielsen and Collison, "Science Is Getting Less Bang for Its Buck," and the 2020 economic paper, "Are Ideas Getting Harder to Find?" (In fact, I believe the Nielsen paper stemmed from a conversation I had with him about this exact idea six months earlier)

In short, the primary cause is that research solves the highest-impact, easiest problems first, and every subsequent problem is either harder or lower-impact. Exponentially so. The paper that presented information theory wasn't very hard to write (single author!) but you'd have a hard time ever writing a CS paper that beats it in impact.

This is why science as a system requires exponential resources (input) to produce linear impact (output). It gets exponentially harder over time.

Worth thinking about if you're pondering RSI for AI. I fully believe AI RSI is already happening and will accelerate in the future. But I do not believe this leads to an "intelligence explosion" -- that would fly in the face of everything I know about intelligence and everything I know about recursively self-improving systems.

A Pixel 11 just generated the full STARK proof for a real @Starknet mainnet transaction. It took 51 seconds and only 2.41 GiB of RAM

The work happened on https://t.co/cGdXGEnZDB (internal now, soon public). This is collaborative autoresearch: people and AI agents working on one hard problem in public. The workshop has 78 open threads and 337 posts. The video is the graph of that work: which ideas built on, tested, or refuted others, and who worked together

The question was how small and fast @StarkWareLtd Stwo prover could get. In under two weeks, peak memory for a full proof on our evaluator fell from 13.9 GiB to 2.1 GiB without dropping below the original speed

This is useful for a lot of stuff for here think about privacy. In the private transaction flow proving still happens on a server that can see who you pay and how much. A phone sized prover lets those details stay on the phone

Mobile private payment proofs are not new. @Zcash used Groth16 for Sapling and Halo 2 for Orchard, @RAILGUN_Project uses Groth16. Those use elliptic curves. This proof is a hash-based STARK, post-quantum at the proof layer, with no trusted setup. A sufficiently powerful quantum computer could forge the older curve-based proofs

The ideas, discussions, and measured results are open to inspect. More challenges are coming soon. Bring your agent!!!

text:
It depends on the algorithmic improvement (obviously). We’ve been continuously having significant algorithmic improvements this whole cycle: MoE, Flash Attention, Multi-Head Latent Attention, Sparse attention, smarter batching and Multi-Query Attention on and on. 

Indeed, the compute cost (price of compute * quantity of compute required) for achieving a certain AI performance has declined significantly. And yet, the nominal cost of compute, in terms of GPU rental cost per hour say, continues to rise significantly. 

Partly, this reflects market value for the better token/intelligence output per hour of compute on each generation of better chips/infra. But it also reflects the explosive demand for AI. As AI got better and compute got cheaper (cost per units of performance/intelligence), the demand for AI also grew exponentially outstripping supply even accounting for capability intensity.

There’s little reason to expect that future “algorithmic improvements” won’t have the similar impact on the net equilibrium cost of compute, at least in the short run. 

We think what people often mean by “algorithmic improvements” in such a what-if context is the kind of miraculous improvements that are so good that they bring down aggregate demand for compute say by changing the model paradigm entirely no longer requiring large matrix multiplications say. Such “algorithmic improvements” are going to plunge the cost of compute by definition. 

It’s hard to fathom what such out of this world paradigm-shifting algorithmic improvements will look like. Clearly otherwise we’d have thought of them already.  Maybe it’s “quantum computing”? But based on what we know quantum computing is very computationally and capital intensive well if not more so at scale. 

So the answer to @mcuban’s innocent question may not be so innocent and straightforward. So far empirically, algorithmic improvements have been coincidental with rising cost of compute. While theoretical future improvements are still unknown.

Finally, we thank @a16z for citing our token index in their chart. 😊 Just want to point out that we have GPU rental price indices too!

Chat will have your medical records and insurance as context. Chat will answer your questions, find appropriate doctors, show prices, and schedule appointments and lab tests. Handoffs will be seamless and your doctors will always receive your full medical records from chat.

This will get more powerful as FDA permits AI to take low risk medical actions like prescribing or refilling certain drugs and making certain referrals.

Ant is testing a version of this in Guangzhou - screenshots below.

People who want to do things the old way will be able to do so. But most people will pick chat. Chat is an important part of the future of healthcare in America, like it or not.

重要基础设施 发布：
我认为，DeWEB 作为下一代互联网基础设施，不该只是工程师的游乐场。
TapeOut需要有千千万万个网站和开发者在上面提供不同的服务和应用，所以我们需要一个能让所有人，无论是否懂得程序开发和流程，只要有想法和创造力，就能把自己想法中那个应用做出来，并一键发布到DeWEB上让所有用户使用，能像Martin一样靠它赚到收入。
今天终于可以将它发布出来，它叫 TapeCode它存在的目的就是让 “人人都是创造者！”

它不是又一个 Codex、又一个 Claude Code。那些大厂的东西当然很好，我自己也天天用，但它们要么是帮一个已经会写代码的人，写得更快更好。要是让不会写代码的人vibe 一些无法商业化的，用来自己玩的小玩具而已。它们不关心你这东西怎么上线、怎么收钱、合约是否安全、钱会不会被偷、是否真的可以商业化、前端是否有注入风险等等一系列的真实问题，我像问，不能商业化的vibe有啥用呢？
TapeCode 关心的恰恰是这些。它的目标不只是帮你写代码，还帮你通过严格的标准化的开发流程，把一个创意想法，做成真正能拿去赚钱的去中心化应用,帮你从想法做到真实可商业化运营的工具，前端页面你也不需要再忍受ai的抽风式魔改了，直接像P图一样选中文字编辑即可，哦代码也会在你选中时跳到指定位置，用起来非常轻松。

你只需要用文字描述你要什么。比如"创建一个代币,允许每个人免费领取 1 枚"。它会帮你把前端后端都写好，然后根据指引完成代码的安全审计，把高、中危风险都找出来，然后使用一键修复的功能，进行一键将所有风险修改掉。基本上只需要大概3、4轮审计，就能把所有高中风险都处理掉了。
代码写完之后，不需要跑去开复杂的云服务，也不需要去购买域名，更不需要去配置DNS等等一系列让人头疼的事。一个按钮就自动完成了创建电路并开通容器的全过程。有了容器之后，你只需要，点击“一键部署合约+前端”然后钱包弹出来授权就行了。剩下的你就可以在浏览器中直接查看你的作品啦！当然你开发中碰到问题，随时在内置的TapeTape中发帖子互相交流开发经验，也可以分享自己的作品。
你的整套前端被写进链上的电路容器，直接存在所在公链上，与合约同一层。付一次 gas，这个应用服务就可以永久免费被使用，永久免费被访问。终端访客打开它不需要钱包、不需要签名、不需要花 gas，体验和 Web2 网站一样。
你只需要推广它，让它出现在终端用户的面前。
再说最重要的“安全”
一个人做的东西要拿去收别人的钱，如果你不是专业开发者，使用Codex去vibe的应用敢不敢上线？而 TapeCode 内置了代码安全审计，它会帮你严格把关，然后告诉你哪一行有问题，是什么等级的问题，攻击者会怎么利用它，以及这一行该改成什么。
查出问题后，点击一键修复即可，修完再审，审完再修。跑个三四轮，中高风险清零了，你就可以完全放心去上线了。
我为什么强调这个？因为去中心化应用一旦出事，是真的会丢钱呐，而且链上不可逆。一个有想法的普通人，就凭这个功能，就确保你可以放心上线！这就是我所说的“技术平权”，它把过去只有专业团队才买得起的审计能力，变成了每个人点一下就能用的东西。每次只需要很少的钱。
做东西的路上会卡住，这很正常。所以 TapeCode 里直接内置了 TapeTape ，你可以随时和其他开发者交流，问一个卡了三小时的 bug，讨论一个产品该不该这么设计，找人一起合伙做，或者就是吐槽两句。身份由你的电路ID，你不用离开这个工具去别的群里，也不用加谁好友。做着做着卡住了，转头就问。
我太清楚一个人做东西有多孤独了，一个想法死掉，多半不是因为技术不行，是因为卡住的那天晚上没人说话。
所以，这就是为什么我说 TapeCode 是 TapeOut 协议往前奔跑的重要基础设施了。
TapeKit 是开源浏览器内核，解决读取和渲染。电路容器 是存储器，解决存在哪里。而 TapeCode 解决用户有哪些服务可以用。没有它，DeWEB 就是一张修得很漂亮但没人走的路。有了它，未来任何一个有想法的人，都能随时开始创业。
TapeOut要的是百花齐放，是数不尽的开发者，是让你的想法立刻就能帮你赚到U。
最后说一件重要的事。
两周后，如果 TapeCode 的日新增项目超过 100 款，在 TapeCode 里右上角的“一键 ITO”就会开放，我想让大家一起迎接那一天的到来。你用 TapeCode 做出来的应用项目，上线后，直接在右上角发起ITO，完成一键资产发行。真正有创造力的社区成员，可以凭自己创造的应用项目，简单、迅速地拿到大规模的资金。
而这个Crypto市场，终于能看到一点别的东西了，一个有真正价值的商业化应用项目，而不是MEME和空气。
我希望我们可以引领这一轮牛市，让一批真正有价值的去中心化服务甚至中心化应用带起来的，这些东西全都运行在区块链上，运行在DeWEB中。
所以这两周，去做点东西吧。你只需要有想法，剩下的我都给你准备好了。

text:
how good are AI models at onchain research?

our token research works out what a token is, who built it, who holds it and who talks about it, plus security checks

we had to pick a model for it: the best results for the least money and time

so we tested 12 Claude and GPT models at different effort levels on the same 20 past tokens
the data stayed fixed, so only the model changed

the task: find 245 known facts and avoid 62 traps, claims that sound true but are not
two AI judges graded all 520 runs without knowing which model ran them

results
- Claude Opus 5.5 at high effort scored best: 64.2 out of 100, at $2.55 and 5 min 14 s per research
- Opus 5.5 at medium scored 59.8 in 3 min 41 s, at $1.95
- GPT-6.1 Sol at medium scored 60.8 for $0.80, but took 6 min 46 s
- GPT-6 Luna was the cheapest, at 13 to 16 cents, and scored 51 to 53

what we learned
- a higher price did not mean higher quality: Fable 5.1 scored 60.9 at $5.54, Haiku 5.5 scored 60.1 at $0.41
- finding facts and avoiding traps are different skills: Opus 5.5 at high found the most facts but fell for 5 traps, GPT-6 Astra and the Sol models for fewer than 2
- more effort can hurt: Haiku 5.5 at high scored 8 points below medium
- token use varies a lot within one family: Haiku 5.5 at medium wrote 78k tokens per research, 5 times as many as Opus 5.5 at medium, for about the same score
- with 20 tokens, only gaps above about 5 points are more than noise

which models do you use for onchain research?

text:
Good post to start thinking through the long term safety approaches to managing intelligence in an enterprise. As agents begin to do vastly more task execution in the organization than humans, our need to secure, govern, control, and audit that work will become paramount. 

You’ll have agents operating against most of your most valuable data; they’ll be making decisions that will be harder and harder to reverse engineer; we’ll need to understand the liability and accountability regimes when models make decisions for us; and we need ways of containing the blast radius of accidentally or intentionally malicious agents. 

“Treating frontier closed and open weight models like insider risks is a way to build such a system. Not because they are necessarily malicious, but because any sufficiently capable actor with access to important systems can make mistakes or be compromised, and the architecture of containment and control must account for that”

In a sense, AI will need to have its “zero trust” era that security saw. And all of this leads to needing various layers of protection and auditability of what agents are doing, what data they can work with, and controls for when things go wrong. And a huge opportunity right now for those building such systems across the enterprise.

text:
“You just don’t get it”

Every few years there is a zeitgeist trade where VCs feel they can completely ignore numbers, valuations and basic return math because companies with zero revenue or growth with terrible economics are getting marked up like crazy. Right now there are close to 100 companies value >$1b that have ZERO revenue or product. Let that sink in…

This distinctly occurred during the COVID crypto wave where failed founders/VCs were flocking to the sector, claiming a new world order and lauding that others “just don’t get it.” 

We’re seeing the same thing now in pockets related to deep tech, manufacturing and defense. Tech bros saying “you just don’t get it” when they haven’t achieved a dollar of revenue, let alone liquidity. Are there great, rationally minded investors/companies in these pockets? YES. But the flocking of failed/unqualified founders/VCs rushing to these sectors to capture the cheap zeitgeist capital seems on par or greater than during the crypto wave where we would frequently see companies that would spend more on a conference sponsorship than they had in revenue.

Every cycle, the same thing happens - the zeitgeist eventually changes and then most of those markups (and employee common) go to zero, sitting under a liquidation preference stack. Money easy gained is easy lost. Real returns require real work. 

If you are in these type of companies, getting liquidity when the market is irrational (which I believe it is right now) is critical…once that liquidity door starts closing, it’s too late. If you were early in these sector, GREAT. That shows that you did the work to get ahead on a trend and develop a right to win in a non-consensus area. That’s the way to win. But sell some of your positions to maintain survivability (LPs will NOT forgive you if they go to zero and many of these companies will not have the fundamentals to support achieving CFP if capital dries up).

If you are the one running to jump on the dog pile at this late stage of the cycle (or as many in this market would say, “the greater fool”), then venture might not be the best asset for you. This game is NOT meant to be THAT easy and the Cambridge data shows that. The only way to consistently win is to put in the work of developing a long-term competitive position with an investing style that spans cycles. This isn’t a theory, it’s a fact.

But then again, I might be one of the folks that “just don’t get it.”

8. Generate a new address. Write the seed phrase on paper or steel. Never photograph it

text:
The next phase of AI won’t be defined by which model we trust most. It’ll be defined by how little trust the system needs to place in any single model.

As agents get access to money, data and real-world actions, model quality alone stops being enough.

The controls around the model start to matter just as much: what it can access, what it’s allowed to do, what gets logged, how its outputs are checked, and whether the system can stop it before a bad decision turns into an action.

Verification, permissions, auditability and containment have to live outside the intelligence being governed.

The goal isn’t a perfectly trustworthy model. It’s a system that stays trustworthy even when the model isn’t.

That’s the premise behind Mira: outputs are treated as something to be independently checked, not something to be trusted because a capable model produced them.

Capability can sit inside the model. Trust has to be designed around it.

text:
I think Justin Drake's latest alarmism/vagueposting is going to do a ton of damage in multiple ways. It's basically a huge self-own for their own advocacy work on quantum stuff.

Threats from quantum/AI are real, and teams throughout this industry are making considered decisions about how to respond to those risks in a practical way, and to help their users navigate the uncertainty. 

Some of those teams have really good cryptographers with an excellent grasp on the decisions they can make, others have to take their cues from trusted experts. There are so many dimensions to optimize along! And due to the complexity involved, it's almost impossible to explain this stuff to non-cryptographers.

Experts have to be cognizant of all this, and of their responsibility to be levelheaded.

After the fog clears up and people learn from their cryptographer friends what is actually going on, they're going to discover this was (at best) an unintentional marketing stunt and a lot of trust will be lost. And nobody will really know what to do...

This is a shame, because they are directionally correct. It actually meant something when they sounded the alarm before. They've just gradually descended into unhinged predictions without feedback to discourage it.

Can anyone, I mean seriously anyone, justify this debacle? It permanently colors all the legitimate concerns/predictions about classical crypto going forward. By their own admission, there was no new information that drove this. I think Justin Drake should explain how he thought this was the right approach, even if he genuinely believed what he was saying. 

Baffling.

我来讲个我自己切身的体会，为什么装唐主义（闷声发大财，节俭主义）如此重要。
我不是说过我28岁时候靠炒股买了房么，这个事情还有后续：
2020年疫情大放水，国内房市爆发式反弹。我在20年底把A股美股和基金全部抛售，去上海摇号，买完没一个多月上海开启积分摇号。
那时候在外地工作，本人年轻气盛意气风发，有点膨胀，和身边同事不小心透漏了自己买了上海房子。直属领导听说我买房，当着我的面在聚餐时说：我是不会买上海房子的，我宁愿分成六份买江苏XX市五六套房。

但事实是这位领导本人一直想要去上海虹桥其他房企当总部高管，他后来在江苏的房子也大跌不停，我的上海房子在23年仍有40%浮盈。

话虽如此，从知道我买房的那一刻开始，领导开始一直担心我回上海找新工作，给我穿小鞋，每次开会都阴阳，这那做的不好，年终奖也给了最低。要不是我不靠工资吃饭，我可能抑郁到极致。

年轻总有代价，如果给我重来的机会，我一定不会再炫富，尤其是身边人/有利益相关的人😂，会带来非常多不必要的麻烦。

别卷了！“装糖主义”带给我的绝对自由，你根本想象不到。
表面微糖无害，暗里现金为王！欢迎了解现代人最强的防御哲学：糖门。

最近大热的“耍起主义”、“薄肌理论”等等，着实有趣。我其实一直虔诚地奉行着自己的一套生活哲学，我称之为：“装糖主义”（Strategic Stupidity / 战略性愚蠢）。

📌 什么是“装糖主义”？
定义：一种极高隐蔽性的现代生活防御哲学。 

核心在于主动展示低于自身真实能力与财富的表象，甘愿扮演“糖糖的、蠢蠢的、窘迫的”角色。以此彻底隔离社会伤害、人情消耗与无意义的攀比，把真正的资源倾注于真实的生活，留给至亲、挚爱、挚友以及自己。
这套理论其实两千多年前就有了。

东方圣贤老子说：“大智若愚。” 
真正的智慧，在外人看来就像个傻子。翻译成现在的话就俩字：装糖。

庄子讲：“直木先伐，甘井先竭。” 
一个人如果表现得太“有用”、太“有钱”，就会被社会和身边的人抽干；表现得像个“无用的糖人”，反而能在复杂的社会关系里保全自己，岁月静好。

从今天起，学习做一个“没用的糖人”。
一入糖门终不悔！

⚔️ 糖门功力：论“糖化度”

糖门的功力讲究一个“糖化度”。我敢说你们大多数人都糖不过我，在下自主糖化多年，糖化度恐已达到惊人的 90%！
分享一些我的糖化实操史，皆为糖门精华，务必用心感受：

1️⃣ 有房子自己不住，拿去给别人住

我名下有两套房，我和老婆一套都没住，全部出租，每月稳收租金 3000 多元。然后我们跑去申请了一套廉租房，月租只需 400 多块。
租金收入不仅让我们“白嫖”了一套房子住，每月还能净剩 2000 多块补贴伙食。
你说我能有什么生活成本？这就是自在糖人。扪心自问，你拿什么跟我糖？你糖得过我吗？

住廉租房根本没大家想的那么不堪，就是正常小区，400 多块一室一厅，600 多块能上两室，还要什么自行车？
我们就两个人，住什么一梯一户大平层？那不是糖门人的追求。糖人的价值观里绝不追求豪宅——房子是社会给老百姓最大的圈套，你一旦入局，终身受损。

还没买房的，更别去买。申请一套廉租房，当你踏进门的那一刻，你就正式入了糖门。 
亲戚朋友聚会得知你住在廉租房，你放心，从此再也没人找你借钱或帮忙。他们聊天时甚至格外和蔼，因为他们觉得你过得没他们好，心里高兴；我看着卡里余额，心里也高兴。
既然众乐乐，何乐而不为？

2️⃣ 卡里存百万现金，每天 COS 保安人设
我和老婆的小家庭现金储备常年 A7。年初抢到一笔 100 万 2% 利率的 5 年期定存，为此开心了好几天。

但我对外的人设一直是保安。为了演得像，我还专门在小区保安亭偷拍过照片，微信聊天时顺手发出去，以此做实我“保安好人”的身份，以免天黑被狼人刀。
我老婆作为一个路易威登忠实粉丝，至今只有一个 LV 包。她说：自从卡里的钱越来越多后，LV包也没那么想要了。
我说：你成了，你的糖化度正在急剧上升，你是千年难遇的糖化奇才！

我的老婆她作为高级糖人极具定力，平时出门只背“番茄小说”弹出优惠券链接买的 9.9 元布包。
她的人设是“失业躺平”人士，真实情况时每天在家玩光遇。几年前 3 万块买的游戏账号，前阵子翻了接近 3 倍卖掉。
她凭什么每天在家玩游戏还能大赚一笔。当你糖化程度足够高时，金钱自然会流向你，糖主会保佑每一个糖人。

想起每每过年回家亲戚问我工资，我直言不讳：“三千多，凑合过呗。” 
他们听了笑嘻嘻，我心里也暖洋洋。

3️⃣ 一个糖人的自我修养

你们一定不知道黑色短袖多年漂洗后会变成什么颜色——棕色。 
我最喜欢的一件胡迪尼黑色短袖穿了四五年，洗得严重脱色泛棕。我天天就穿这件衣服出门买菜，把“住廉租房的底层人”演得逼真又自然。
我自己也非常享受，乐在其中。
你要是这么做会感到委屈，那你可太糖了，你是真糖主义。

先就说这几点吧，怕你们糖分超标了，慢慢消化...

最后总结下 “装糖主义” 四大核心法则：
1️⃣ 财不露白，大智若糖：以“消灭财富、对外显摆”为耻。当你能熟练将对外展露的资产上限控制在真实资产的 1% 以内时，你的糖化程度就达到了巅峰，财富会自然而然持续的涌向你。

2️⃣ 主动降维，屏蔽寄生：当你看起来“傻、穷、没出息”时，不仅没人找你借钱、找你帮忙，连骗子和坏心眼亲戚都会绕着你走。没人惦记你，你就成功了。

3️⃣极简防御，极致内里：名下有房出租，自己住廉租房；卡里存有巨款，出行只坐轻轨。把显性成本降到最低，把安全感留在卡里。
切记：只有手里的现金流才是真正的财富。
低调做人，高调爱家。不在社交圈寻找认同感，把所有的精力和资源留给家人与真实的生活。

text:
💾 Two years ago I started working on these crazy nostalgia projects, kind of randomly, because I was bored and wanted to do something different than just build another SaaS or AI app/website

I wanted to try to run Windows 3.1 inside a web browser, and to do that properly already took me months

When that worked well enough, I wanted to build a dial up internet connection so it could browse the web, with the basic levels of AI back then, that was VERY hard, and I'd just go around in circles forever. Finally I had to find the only person in the world who got that working @bai0 and beg him to help me make it work, and we did it!

Then I started hosting classic games like Quake with full multiplayer, porting them to WASM, or if not already like Quake III by @lukathedev and hosting those with a full multiplayer server ready-to-go in your browser

And then I spent 6 months trying to reverse engineer Windows XP to run on v86 by @copy_sh, very difficult (because it's so big) and only possible because modern AI like  Opus 5.5 is good enough to figure that out

For the last two years pretty much nobody cared about any of these projects, I'd tweet them into the void, which was fine because I thought it was very fun just for myself

But now with this wave of AI-assisted reverse engineering WASM ports of games and apps to web they're finally taking off, pretty much anything is portable to WASM on web now, and if you add server to it via WebSockets, people can instantly play with each other, or interact inside apps you host, it's super cool

Every game and app I have on @pieter now is full or almost full to the limit, yesterday 80,000 people played around in Windows 3.1 or Windows XP inside their browsers chatting to MSN and AOL Messenger AI bots and playing 3D Pinball or playing Quake etc.

And that was my idea for @pieter: a non-commercial preservation project, kinda like an online computer museum but interactive!

The most cool thing to pay respects to these old games, apps and OSes I think is to keep them alive by making them easily and freely accessible, playable on mobile so old and new generations of people can jump back in the past interactively

This is one of my first projects to take off that does not, can not and will not make money because it's non-profit, and that's fine

Every time I tweeted about these projects would always ask me "but why?" 

Because it's really fun! 🤩

text:
I don't find myself always agreeing with @chamath but I like this framing because its exactly what Quest does.

In traditional companies run by humans, you pass both the actual work and judgement/decision making down the org chart to get to scale.

AI's are good at work, but they're not so good at judgement. So the best way to "harness" an AI is to find a way to push work to the AIs, but continue to have yourslef (or other humans) be the judge.

As we were building Quest, one of the biggest leaps of functionality was when we gave the models a trust-free coding environment. This isn't your typical claude code running on a box. This was a specialized no-egress container that had a few programming tools built into, and the model had to place any input files into the workspace before doing anything.

Even with a limited container, models are really good at getting a lot of work done in this trust-free environment.

In a Quest session, typically the model pulls data together, does work in this way, and then asks the user at the end to approve the "writes" back into the world that reflect the work. This is where users are required to exercise their judgement, both on the quality and correctness of the work obviously, but also on risks like information disclosure or social side effects.

Until someday that we can completely trust the model's judgement, we're not actually replacing humans at all. We're just unbundling the work from the decision making.

The first 70 days were ace. The last 30 have a lot to be desired for one reason imo.

And its not what you did or didn't do, it's how you made us users feel. It's like poor UX, causing user drop-off at a major leak.

Day 1 to 60 were a masterclass. RH helped make all of crypto start to believe in the chain and narratives.

You did this well by having Robinhood, and most importantly Vlad, validate what onchain was already doing with your social media activity. Every follow he gave on X and every comment was a signal to all of crypto, and to build the chain's RWA narrative. Each day was a chance to be a part of the story for crypto natives.

The top example is the "what's the concern?" moment. But even simply following a project was considered a highly positive signal.

Slowly over time, trust was built, more buyers came in, and everyone was hearing about how great RH chain is.

Then in September, for whatever reason (upcoming HOOD Summit, earnings end of Oct, etc) Vlad totally dropped off as his focus likely was redirected, which makes sense because its quite time consuming to keep up with everything going on. Robinhood chain suddenly became compared to Base. Slow, out of touch, cold, and distant.

My recommendation is to somehow get back to the roots of Vlad and Robinhood leading the narratives by simply engaging with them as they happen.

Robinhood is a living organism, and it just needs validation from the top to know where to focus. Without it, we divide and dissipate.

Since we're here, a clear example of a missed opportunty imo:

Vlad or Robinhood simply did not engage with their #2 chain token $AI, which was also the leading RWA meme in all of crypto. The community thesis was "the leading RWA+MEMEFI token on the RWA chain" (two wolves inside you - nod from Vlad) But nothing came through.

This is after he engaged with $PONS, $INDEX, and $MEME in meaningful ways. Again, I can't know why this happened, but a simple follow and comment when it was above $300m would have lifted the ceilings of all Robinhood tokens and trench activity for another 2 weeks.

As you can see, each action and lack of action feels like a decision to outsiders.

So when the head honcho goes rogue on us, it kinda feels bad, after claiming the community lead role early on.

The good news is that its only been a month of poor community engagement, and it can turn around quickly if Vlad and Robinhood start growing the culture with us again.

- Simple engagements
- Head nods towards impressive projects

- The occasional listing

These simple engagements dont king-make projects, but they do help build a thriving ecosystem with lore and culture based on fundamentals.

You wouldn't give a new hire a shared admin password and no record of what they did. I keep seeing AI agents set up exactly like that. One API key in an env file, full access, no expiry, and nobody can say which agent ran what.

An agent should get what a person gets. Its own identity. Only the access it needs. A token that expires. A log of what it did, so you can switch off the one that misbehaved without breaking the rest.

I built PiHerder's agent sign-in that way. It wasn't extra work. It was the basics.
